detail.title: Institutional Voids, Managerial Cognition, and Data-Driven Competitive Advantage: A Conceptual Framework for SME Digital Transformation in Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies face a paradoxical challenge: the institutional environments in which they operate simultaneously generate demand for data-driven decision-making and impede the development of the capabilities required to deliver it. Existing frameworks for understanding SME digital transformation draw predominantly on developed-economy contexts and treat institutional conditions as background noise rather than theoretically significant contingencies. This paper addresses that gap by developing an integrative conceptual framework that positions managerial cognition as the critical mediating mechanism through which institutional voids shape digital transformative capability and, ultimately, data-driven competitive advantage. Drawing on institutional theory, managerial cognition theory, dynamic capability theory, and the resource-based view, we argue that institutional voids primarily affect digital capability development through their distortion of managerial information environments, producing heterogeneous cognitive schemas about digital technology potential. Managers who engage in active sensemaking processes develop more accurate mental models, enabling digital resource mobilisation even under conditions of institutional constraint. Digital transformative capability, once developed, creates the organisational preconditions for analytics capability—a sequential dependency with important theoretical and practical implications. Six formal research propositions are advanced, specifying testable relationships between institutional void intensity, managerial sensemaking, digital transformative capability, analytics capability, and competitive advantage. The framework contributes to digital transformation theory by centring cognition in the SME capability-building process and extends institutional theory by providing a microlevel mechanism that accounts for firm-level heterogeneity in institutionally void environments.

detail.abstract: The prevailing paradigm in artificial intelligence, cognitive modeling, and generative physics simulation is bounded by a fundamental thermodynamic and computational constraint: the irreversible loss of information. As sequence lengths increase and simulation horizons expand, conventional autoregressive architectures and numerical integrators suffer from unrecoverable computational drift, catastrophic forgetting, and algorithmic opacity. The inability to execute perfect, atomic rollbacks introduces systemic model risk, rendering current architectures increasingly incompatible with emerging enterprise governance and regulatory mandates. To resolve this critical limitation, this whitepaper introduces the Unified Reversible Intelligence Substrate (URIP) Engine. The URIP Engine is a mathematically precise, deterministic framework that harmonizes continuous physics simulation and discrete cognitive reasoning within a unified, machine-precision reversible architecture. The engine combines two highly specialized subsystems: the Deterministic Generative Physics Engine (DGPE v3) and the Universal Inference Graph (UIG), anchored by a shared Deterministic General Intelligence Core (DGIC-style) substrate. By structuring computation as a purely bijective, geometry-native process utilizing orthogonal rotation-matrix cores and fixed-point arithmetic protocols, the URIP Engine natively eliminates model drift. Empirical evaluation provides verifiable evidence of the architecture's stability: DGPE v3 maintains strict energy conservation with structural drift bounded between and , achieving exact reversibility after 50 forward and 50 inverse steps. Simultaneously, the UIG component demonstrates a reversibility error of across symbolic explanation chains and probabilistic hypothesis updates, despite utilizing a highly compressed (1, 32) latent state. This comprehensive report exhaustively details the mathematical foundations, system architecture, empirical results, and adversarial resilience of the URIP Engine, establishing it as an audit-grade, SR 26-2 compliant framework necessary for the future of financial risk modeling, scientific simulation, and high-stakes autonomous systems.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the effects of the 2021-2022 energy crisis on energy use and economic performance of manufacturing plants in Norway. For identification, we exploit a natural experiment where limited transmission capacity generated spatial variation in electricity price increases across pricing zones. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that plants exposed to the price shock reduced electricity consumption by about 9%, corresponding to an own-price elasticity of approximately 0.09. This estimate lies at the lower end of previously reported elasticities, suggesting that responses may differ for large shocks. On average, we find no evidence of adverse effects on economic performance. However, for the most electricity-intensive plants, we document modest negative effects on output and employment, highlighting the importance of accounting for differences in exposure when considering policy responses.

title: Fiscal Multipliers and Sectoral Government Spending in Heterogeneous Production Networks

detail.title: Fiscal Multipliers and Sectoral Government Spending in Heterogeneous Production Networks
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether fiscal multipliers depend on the sectoral allocation of government spending, and how this effect varies with the strength of production network linkages. Using annual data for 68 countries from 1995 to 2020, I construct two indicators: (i) an upstreamness index of government demand, based on the standardized Katz-Bonacich centrality of the sectors receiving public spending, and (ii) the Average Output Multiplier (AOM), which captures the overall strength of input-output linkages within the economy. I estimate state-dependent local projection regressions that allow fiscal multipliers to vary with both the sectoral allocation of spending and the strength of production networks. The results show that directing government demand toward relatively upstream sectors reduces fiscal multipliers, but only in economies with strong production linkages. In weakly connected production networks, the sectoral composition of spending has little or no effect on aggregate output. Quantitatively, within strong-linkage economies, a one-standard-deviation increase in the upstreamness of government demand lowers the multiplier by about 10.6 percent. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for production network structures, which are heterogeneous across countries, when assessing the aggregate effects of fiscal policy and its sectoral allocation.

detail.abstract: This study reexamines herding behaviour in financial markets by leveraging a multiframework research design that integrates traditional dispersion-based models with a novel performance-driven framework named as Relative Performance Convergence Index (RPCI). Daily closing stocks data of 69 firms (FTSE 100) over the period 2018-2026 is used. Herding is initially examined using the Cross-Sectional Standard Deviation (CSSD) and Cross-Sectional Absolute Deviation (CSAD) models. Both dispersion-based frameworks fail to detect statistically significant evidence of herding and fails to capture directional & dynamic adjustment processes and instead show increasing dispersion during market stress period thus highlighting a key empirical inconsistency in case of developed markets and pointing toward misrepresentation of investors behaviour. To address this limitation, this study introduces the Relative Performance Convergence Index (RPCI), which conceptualises herding as a dynamic process in which underperforming assets adjust toward outperforming assets over time. The empirical results indicate that while herding is not persistent across the full sample, the RPCI reveals strong and statistically significant convergence behaviour during the crisis period. Findings indicate that herding is time-varying and state-dependent. By bridging the gap between behavioural theory and empirical evidence, the study provides a more comprehensive framework for identifying herding in financial markets.

detail.title: A Hybrid Unsupervised Rating System for Algorithmic Traders in Cryptocurrency Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a hybrid unsupervised rating system to evaluate and classify algorithmic traders operating in cryptocurrency markets. Traditional performance metrics such as the Sharpe Ratio, the Treynor Ratio, and Morningstar-style ratings are shown to be inadequate for high-frequency, non-linear trading environments characterised by fat-tailed return distributions, continuous operation, and extreme volatility. To overcome these limitations, we develop a multi-layer ensemble framework that combines four unsupervised learning models-K-Means, Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), an Autoencoder coupled with K-Means, and DBSCAN-with an individual composite scoring mechanism and a probabilistic fusion stage. 

Using a sample of 85 algorithmic traders collected from the Binance platform (March-April 2025), this proof of concept demonstrates that the proposed framework produces a four-tier rating (Very bad, Bad, Good, Very good) through quartile-based assignment of a continuous Fusion Score (FS). Validation relies on Spearman rank correlations, Kruskal-Wallis tests, and Cohen's d effect sizes, all evaluated within the observed sample to assess internal consistency and discriminative validity. The Sharpe Ratio exhibits a strong monotone relationship with the rating (ρ = 0.771, p < 0.001; d = 2.183 [95% CI: 1.81, 3.09]), and the maximum drawdown decreases monotonically across tiers (d =-1.992 [95% CI:-3.18,-1.42]). Crucially, a direct comparison with a Sharpe Ratio quartile-ranking baseline shows that the hybrid system achieves 2.33× greater MDD discrimination (H hybrid = 26.64 vs H Sharpe = 11.43, Cohen's d =-1.99 vs-0.76), demonstrating that the proposed framework captures risk-adjusted information unavailable to any univariate ranking and establishing a reproducible baseline for future predictive validation. The null hypothesis is rejected at the 1% significance level (FDR-corrected). Notably, principal component analysis reveals that the first component explains 97.4% of total variance in the dataset, providing structural evidence that the multi-metric feature space is dominated by a single quality dimension-which the Fusion Score is designed to capture and partition.

title: Megacities and Human Progress
affiliations: China West Normal University

detail.title: Megacities and Human Progress
detail.abstract: This article examines the rapid growth of megacities and their impact on human progress. It highlights that cities now house nearly half the world's population, with 33 megacities globally. Using China's urbanization experience as a key example, the article shows how policy-driven growth has lifted millions out of poverty while also creating challenges like inequality and pollution. It argues that good governance—focused on sustainability, inclusion, and long-term planning—can turn megacities into engines of opportunity rather than disorder.

title: How Uncertain are Default Rates? The Role of Serial Correlation
affiliations: Raiffeisen Bank International

detail.title: How Uncertain are Default Rates? The Role of Serial Correlation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no competing financial interests
declarations.funderStatement: no funding

detail.abstract: The long-run average default rate (LRADR) is a centrepiece of modern banking regulation. An expression for the estimator's variance that accounts for both cross-sectional and serial correlations of default rates has not been proposed, however. In this article, we derive the variance of the LRADR under both types of correlations. We also obtain a closedform expression of the Fisher information matrix for a large, homogeneous portfolio. The resulting Cramér-Rao lower bound can serve as a benchmark for estimator uncertainty for the probability of default. Using U.S. bank failure data, we find that the serial correlation of failure rates is substantial, resulting in a standard error for the LRADR that is comparable to the estimate itself. Consequently, the LRADR cannot be estimated precisely for such portfolios. Finally, we derive a prediction interval for default rates for use in out-of-time forecasting.

title: Beyond Herding: Evidence of Investor Divergence and Nonlinear Dispersion in the FTSE 100

detail.title: Beyond Herding: Evidence of Investor Divergence and Nonlinear Dispersion in the FTSE 100

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants; ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This study reexamines herding behaviour in financial markets by focusing on dispersion dynamics under market stress. Using the Cross-Sectional Absolute Deviation (CSAD) framework, the results provide no evidence of herding in the FTSE 100 market. Instead, return dispersion increases with larger market movements, indicating heterogeneous investor behaviour rather than convergence. Market volatility is also found to significantly amplify dispersion, suggesting that uncertainty leads to greater behavioural divergence. 

To further explore these dynamics, a machine learning approach is employed. The results indicate that dispersion patterns are nonlinear and time-varying, while predictive performance remains weak, highlighting the complexity and instability of investor behaviour. 

Overall, the findings suggest that, under the conditions examined, market stress is associated with fragmentation rather than coordination. The study contributes by emphasising dispersion as an informative behavioural outcome and by combining econometric and machine learning approaches to capture dynamic market behaviour.

title: India's Short-Term Rental Boom and the Regulatory Risk Nobody Is Pricing In
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: India's Short-Term Rental Boom and the Regulatory Risk Nobody Is Pricing In
detail.abstract: India's short-term rental market is valued at USD 2.39 billion in 2025 and is expanding quickly, but it operates in a near-complete regulatory vacuum. This report looks at the structural risks this lack of policy creates for hosts, host-enablement companies, and investors. It draws on global case studies from New York, Barcelona, Lisbon, and Florence, as well as India's own online gaming regulatory history. The report shows that sudden government action is not a distant possibility but an inevitable part of the market. Primary survey data gathered from active Indian short-term rental hosts adds to the analysis by providing insights into income distribution, platform preferences, management practices, and regulatory awareness. A financial model that compares service-based and software-based host-enablement businesses under regulatory pressure shows that neither model is fully resilient. However, software-driven companies have a clearer path for recovery. The report concludes that stakeholders who consider regulatory preparedness a key business strategy, rather than an afterthought, will be better positioned to survive and adjust when India's policy landscape changes.

title: Optimization Methodologies for Affine-Maximizer Mechanisms

detail.title: Optimization Methodologies for Affine-Maximizer Mechanisms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: This paper develops optimization methodologies for mechanism design in allocation environments with monetary transfers. It defines affine maximizers with Clarke pivot monetary transfers (AM-CPMT) and establishes dominant-strategy incentive compatibility, ex post individual rationality under non-involvement normalization, zero transfers for non-involved agents, and uniqueness of the Clarke pivot transfer under the stated normalization. The paper then formulates finite-scenario models for optimizing mechanism parameters, including agent weights, outcome-adjustment terms, surplus-adjustment terms, adopted outcomes, and induced payments, as quadratically constrained mixed-integer programs. To solve these models, it develops McCormick-envelope relaxations, EPIR and DSIC cuts, fast projected x-p bounds, spatial branch-and-bound, scenario generation, and a hybrid branch-and-bound framework with scenario generation. A second mechanism class, weighted surplus welfare maximizers with Clarke pivot monetary transfers (WSWM-CPMT), is introduced to address recipient payment nonnegativity while preserving the central truthfulness and individual-rationality properties. Overall, the paper provides a computational optimization framework for designing incentive-compatible mechanisms that also satisfy operational payment requirements.

title: Algorithmic Reputation Equivalence (ARE): A Methodology for Developing AI Decision-Stage Equivalents of Human Brand Reputation Measurement Frameworks
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Algorithmic Reputation Equivalence (ARE): A Methodology for Developing AI Decision-Stage Equivalents of Human Brand Reputation Measurement Frameworks
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Reputation Equivalence (ARE), a methodology for constructing AI decision-stage measurement instruments that are structurally and metrically equivalent to existing human-perception brand reputation measurement frameworks. Where established reputation frameworks measure how human populations perceive a brand across defined dimensions using survey methodology, an ARE-derived instrument measures how AI language model reasoning chains resolve brand outcomes across the same dimensions at the purchase decision stage. We define the formal requirements for dimensional equivalence, describe a calibration methodology for establishing cross-instrument score comparability, and introduce the Reputation Gap as the primary derived metric-the signed divergence between a brand's human-perception reputation score and its AI decision reputation score on the same scale. We demonstrate that high human reputation scores do not predict high AI decision reputation scores, that the two instruments capture categorically distinct phenomena, and that the gap between them constitutes a commercially significant and currently unmeasured risk. This paper establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for ARE as a category of measurement. The specific application of ARE to any named proprietary reputation framework requires that framework's dimensional definitions and calibration data as inputs, and must be undertaken in collaboration with the framework's owner.

title: Laffer Curve Under Code Constraints

detail.title: Laffer Curve Under Code Constraints

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest Statement: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. This study is an independent theoretical research and did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how code constraints provided by the decentralized financial market infrastructure (dFMI) alter the inflation‑tax space of sovereign states. When economic agents are able to obtain liquidity outside the traditional banking system via the dFMI, the government’s control over the inflation‑tax base is constrained by this code‑based external mechanism. Within a small open economy framework, we parameterize this constraint and show that, by depressing demand for the domestic currency and amplifying its sensitivity to inflation, it systematically compresses both the peak and the feasible range of the seigniorage Laffer curve. Our analysis of the asymmetry of this constraint mechanism shows that, in the case of the United States, it operates as an “internal reallocation under a common unit of account”: as the United States exports dollar liquidity through the on‑chain dollar system, it simultaneously draws a rigid upper bound on its own high‑inflation paths. By contrast, for economies whose domestic currency is not the U.S. dollar, the constraint takes the form of external competition across units of account, subjecting the domestic‑currency tax base to more asymmetric structural pressures.

title: Persistence in Demand Fluctuations and Tacit Collusion: Experimental Evidence
affiliations: University of Limassol and University of Cyprus - Department of Economics

detail.title: Persistence in Demand Fluctuations and Tacit Collusion: Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract: We study how the persistence of demand fluctuations affects firms' ability to sustain tacit collusion. Building on Bagwell and Staiger (1997), we develop a discrete dynamic duopoly model and analyze environments with persistent booms, persistent recessions, and transitory demand fluctuations. This demand structure allows us to isolate the effect of persistent demand growth on strategic decisions, while abstracting from other sources of uncertainty. We derive conditions under which both procyclical and countercyclical pricing can be sustained in equilibrium. Guided by this theoretical framework, we conduct a laboratory experiment. The experimental results show that persistent positive demand shocks lead to higher prices than persistent negative demand shocks, whereas under transitory demand fluctuations, pricing behavior depends on the demand trajectory faced by subjects. Overall, the evidence suggests that subjects condition their behavior not only on the current state of demand, but also on their beliefs about how demand will evolve over time. Subjects appear to be more willing to cooperate when future demand conditions are expected to be more favorable.

title: Ghost Performers in Machine Simulacra: Neighbouring Rights Protection of Digital Twins
affiliations: and Wuhan University

detail.title: Ghost Performers in Machine Simulacra: Neighbouring Rights Protection of Digital Twins

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: This article asks what law should protect when artificial-intelligence-driven digital twins function as machine simulacra. Digital twins are not static models. They are live simulations that interpret, predict, and optimize physical systems. Because their value lies in ongoing performance rather than a fixed work, copyright, patent, and trade secret law fit them poorly. The article argues for a new sui generis neighbouring right centred on performance. To address the artificial-intelligence system's lack of legal personality, it distinguishes that system as the Factual Performer and the human or corporate controller as the Performance Principal. Using Baudrillard's theory of simulacra, the article explains how protection can follow the twin from faithful replica to hyperreal model without producing legal hyperreality. Rights remain anchored in human control and responsibility rather than in the simulacrum as a work.

title: The Impact of Personal Remittance on Economic Growth in Sri Lanka: An Autoregressive Distributed Lag Bound Test
affiliations: University of Vavuniya and University of Vavuniya

detail.title: The Impact of Personal Remittance on Economic Growth in Sri Lanka: An Autoregressive Distributed Lag Bound Test
detail.abstract: The study explores the impact of personal remittances on the economic growth of Sri Lanka from 1980 to 2021. The Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) technique is employed to analyze both long-term and short-term effects of personal remittances on the country's economic growth. Findings revealed a positive and statistically significant influence of personal remittances on long-term economic growth. However, no short-term causal relationship between the two variables was observed. Further, it was noted that outward labor migration does not have a significant impact on economic growth either in the long or short run. On the other hand, the study confirmed that gross fixed capital formation significantly and positively contributes to economic growth in both temporal dimensions though foreign direct investment and had a negative but statistically insignificant impact on the long-term economic growth. Moreover, the study underscored the critical role of gross fixed capital formation as a determinant of economic growth, emphasizing its significance both in the long and short run. The study implications highlight the importance of effectively leveraging remittances to foster the economic growth of the country. The intention is to provide valuable insights to the government and policymakers, aiding them in formulating domestic policies for the management of migration from Sri Lanka and strategic utilization of remittances for the country's benefit.

title: Self-Help in International Anarchy: Assessing Global Readiness

detail.title: Self-Help in International Anarchy: Assessing Global Readiness

detail.abstract: Fearing that China's "possession of the modern instruments of industry" would be a "threat to the rest of mankind" and that Russia might "unilaterally" become "the defender of world peace and champion of the United Nations," US analysts developed the idea of "self-help in international anarchy." This essay examines each UN member's stance on a potential global anarchy and their capacity for self-help in such a scenario. It uses all countries’ basic information and military expenditure data from the World Bank, UNGA voting data from the United Nations, and arms trade data from SIPRI.

title: Modeling the Impacts of Reciprocal Tariffs on the 2025 Iowa Economy

detail.title: Modeling the Impacts of Reciprocal Tariffs on the 2025 Iowa Economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Crespi, J.M., C.E. Hart, D.J. Hayes, and L.L. Schulz. 2025. “Modeling the Impacts of Reciprocal Tariffs on the 2025 Iowa Economy.” Policy brief 25-PB 48. Center for Agricultural and Rural Development, Iowa State University.

detail.abstract:
In this analysis, researchers affiliated with the Iowa State University Center for Agricultural and Rural Development use historical trade patterns, elasticities, and revenue linkages to discern the potential 2025 tariffs’ near-term impacts on the state of Iowa. The main results of the study are as follows.
• We examine three hypothetical tariff retaliations by trading nations. In this report, we assume all nations respond in-kind to US tariffs. We recognize that countries may not respond at all, however, at the date of this report, we are merely assessing possibilities.
o Base10 Scenario: a global 10% tariff, with exceptions for Canada and Mexico;
o Reciprocal Scenario: Base10 with the additional reciprocal tariffs announced between April 2, 2025 and July 11, 2025; and,
o BRICS Scenario: Reciprocal scenario with additional tariff announcements for BRICS countries.
• Overall losses to Iowa’s Soybean industry of $191 million in the Base10 Scenario to $1.49 billion in the BRICS Scenario; Iowa soybeans are a $5.8 billion industry.
• Overall losses to Iowa’s Corn industry of $126 (Base10) to $528 million (BRICS); Iowa corn is an $11.7 billion industry.
• Overall losses to Iowa’s Hog industry of $200 million (Base10) to $1.18 billion (BRICS); Iowa hog production is a $7.3 billion industry.
• Overall losses to Iowa’s Ethanol industry of $40 (Base10) to $168 million (BRICS); Iowa ethanol is a $7.4 billion industry.
• Revenue losses in these industries translate into additional lost revenues in other industries and lost income, as well as impact the value added (GDP) of the state of Iowa. The ranges in this report reflect total output (revenue) losses to Iowa businesses from $813 million in the Base10 scenario to $4.9 billion in the BRICS scenario. Lost household income ranges from $164 million to $1 billion depending on the scenario. Value added (GDP) is reduced by $396 million in the Base10 scenario to $2.46 billion in the BRICS scenario.
• Tax revenue losses (local, state and federal) range from $56 million to $348 million depending on the scenario. The State of Iowa itself loses from $12 million to $76 million in tax receipts.

title: Divergence Transitions in Financial Markets: A Hierarchical Variance Decomposition Reveals the Inversion of the Cross-domain Fragility Signature
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Divergence Transitions in Financial Markets: A Hierarchical Variance Decomposition Reveals the Inversion of the Cross-domain Fragility Signature
detail.abstract: I test whether a hierarchical variance decomposition of cross-asset returns-separating within-asset temporal variability from between-asset mean trajectory divergence-provides early warning of financial crises. The Signal Ratio (SR), predicted by cross-domain fragility theory to rise before system failure, is instead anti-predictive: AUC = 0.441 across six major crises over 2000-2024. The Divergence Index (DI), the between-asset component, is the strongest pre-crisis predictor (AUC = 0.573, p = 3.2 × 10⁻⁶), outperforming VIX (0.552), realized volatility (0.544), and cross-sectional dispersion (0.517, not significant). Financial crises are divergence transitions-sector trajectories structurally pull apart before collective collapse-in contrast to convergence transitions documented in oncology and electoral forecasting. The decomposition maps onto the distinction between disruptive and stabilizing selection, yielding an early-warning framework whose output direction encodes crisis type.

title: Unlocking Data: A Matrix of Data Sharing Regulation in the Age of AI
affiliations: and Sapir Academic College, School of Law

detail.title: Unlocking Data: A Matrix of Data Sharing Regulation in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: This article addresses the challenges in formulating data-sharing regulations by proposing a systematic regulatory matrix based on data characteristics. While data-driven innovation drives economic growth, existing legal frameworks in the EU are incoherent and often tend toward data propertisation, even if indirectly, which may lead to data underutilisation. The matrix is built on varied data characteristics, and it aims to foster access to data and data-sharing as a fundamental general principle underpinning the data-driven innovation market. This framework offers a balanced regulatory scheme ranging from open access to proprietary models, aiming to maximise innovation and public good in the emerging field of data law.

title: The Cost of Being a Good Girl: Why Being "Nice" May Be Undermining Women's Psychological Well-Being
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Cost of Being a Good Girl: Why Being "Nice" May Be Undermining Women's Psychological Well-Being

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial interests, personal relationships, institutional affiliations, or competing interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual paper based exclusively on published literature and secondary sources. No human participants, personal data, surveys, interviews, or experimental procedures were involved. Therefore, ethical approval was not required for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was conducted independently by the author and received no external funding from any public, commercial, or non-profit organization.

detail.abstract: In many societies, women are socialized from an early age to prioritize harmony, compliance, and the emotional needs of others. Traits such as kindness, self-sacrifice, agreeableness, and emotional availability are frequently rewarded and reinforced, contributing to the development of what is commonly referred to as the “good girl” identity. While these characteristics are often viewed as socially desirable, excessive adherence to them may carry significant psychological costs. This paper explores how chronic people-pleasing behaviors, approval-seeking tendencies, and difficulties in establishing personal boundaries influence the psychological well-being of adult women. Using a qualitative conceptual analysis approach, this study integrates theoretical perspectives from socialization theory, self-concept development, boundary theory, attachment theory, and psychological well-being literature. The analysis examines how repeated patterns of self-suppression, emotional labor, and external validation-seeking can contribute to stress, emotional exhaustion, reduced self-worth, identity diffusion, and diminished life satisfaction. The paper further argues that many women are not necessarily taught how to pursue personal fulfillment, but rather how to gain acceptance through accommodation and self-sacrifice. The findings suggest that the pursuit of being perceived as “nice” may create a paradox in which social approval is achieved at the expense of authenticity and psychological health. While prosocial behaviors and empathy remain important aspects of healthy social functioning, the inability to establish boundaries can transform kindness into a mechanism of self-neglect. This study proposes an integrated conceptual framework demonstrating how social expectations, people-pleasing tendencies, boundary difficulties, and external validation dependency interact to influence adult women's well-being. The paper contributes to the growing literature on gender socialization and psychological well-being by highlighting the hidden costs of excessive niceness and emphasizing the importance of boundary development, self-definition, and authentic self-expression in fostering long-term psychological health.

title: Competitive Tendering for Renewables and Industrial Decarbonisation

detail.title: Competitive Tendering for Renewables and Industrial Decarbonisation

detail.abstract: Competitive tendering of state aid is a tool for governments to ensure that aid is awarded efficiently and at the least cost for public finances. In the context of aid for investment in renewables and industrial decarbonisation, competitive bidding offers important advantages over administratively set support schemes: it improves cost-effectiveness by keeping support close to each project's funding gap; it enhances efficiency by selecting the projects with the highest social value; and it supports transparency, limiting the scope for regulatory capture. This note discusses auction and contract design principles, with an emphasis on how to ensure effective competition and on recent developments in addressing bidder and project heterogeneity, risk, and multi-source funding.

title: When She Fails: Women Entrepreneurs and Gender Gaps in Business Bankruptcy
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University, University of Delaware, Rutgers Business School and Rutgers Business School at Newark and New Brunswick

detail.title: When She Fails: Women Entrepreneurs and Gender Gaps in Business Bankruptcy
detail.abstract: Female-owned firms are more likely to be pushed into liquidation and less likely to emerge successfully from bankruptcy than observably similar male-owned firms, and the gap widens sharply when courts are congested. In our data on U.S. small-business bankruptcies, female-owned firms are 24 percent more likely to file under Chapter 7 and, conditional on Chapter 11, are considerably less likely to receive a discharge. Evidence from 1.9 million SBA loan records shows little difference in observable pre-filing credit quality between female-and male-owned firms, weakening a simple creditworthiness explanation. This discharge penalty is concentrated among high-caseload judges. Eventstudy evidence around unexpected judicial departures, which raise surviving judges' workloads, shows the female gap widening after vacancy shocks. Women also respond on the filing margin, turning to Chapter 7 more often in congested courts, while experienced attorneys partly offset this avoidance without closing the discharge gap. The evidence points to a post-failure institutional friction in entrepreneurship.

title: Human Capital Loss Among Belarusian and Ukrainian Migrants to the EU
affiliations: BEROC,  and BEROC

detail.title: Human Capital Loss Among Belarusian and Ukrainian Migrants to the EU
detail.abstract: This policy brief examines the underutilization of human capital among involuntary migrants from Ukraine and Belarus in Poland and Lithuania. Focusing on those who migrated after 2020 (Belarus) and 2022 (Ukraine), the brief investigates the factors influencing the conversion of their pre-migration skills into gainful employment in their host countries. Our findings show that despite many migrants possessing high levels of education and professional qualifications, structural barriers and low convertibility of their skills, hinder their full labor market integration. This skill underutilization not only limits migrants' professional growth and earning potential but also deprives the host countries of valuable skills and potential economic gains.

title: Climate-Induced Agricultural Losses in Jammu & Kashmir An Applied Econometric Analysis of Flood Impacts on Farmers (2023-2025)
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Climate-Induced Agricultural Losses in Jammu & Kashmir An Applied Econometric Analysis of Flood Impacts on Farmers (2023-2025)
detail.abstract: This paper examines the agricultural impact of extreme flood events in Jammu & Kashmir (J&K) during 2023-2025, a period marked by severe climate-induced disasters. Using a Difference-inDifferences (DiD) econometric framework and publicly available data from government disaster reports, agricultural census records, and meteorological sources, we estimate the causal effect of flood exposure on crop yields, farm income, and food security for smallholder farmers across affected districts. Our analysis focuses on key crops including paddy rice, maize, apple horticulture, and saffron-the primary agricultural outputs of the region. Results indicate that flood-affected districts experienced a statistically significant decline in crop output, with paddy yields falling by an estimated 35-45% in severely inundated areas relative to comparable non-affected regions. The paper further documents heterogeneous impacts across elevation zones and crop types, with horticultural crops suffering disproportionately large losses. These findings carry important implications for agricultural policy, climate adaptation strategies, and disaster compensation mechanisms in ecologically fragile Himalayan economies.

title: GPU-aligned Deterministic Scaling in a Reversible Intelligence Substrate

detail.title: GPU-aligned Deterministic Scaling in a Reversible Intelligence Substrate

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or organizational conflicts of interest related to the research, development, or presentation of this work. No external parties influenced the study design, analysis, or conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, clinical data, or sensitive personal information. All experiments were computational in nature; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
The scaling of artificial intelligence architectures to accommodate extreme sequence lengths represents one of the most profound challenges in contemporary computational research. At the core of this challenge lies the fundamental incompatibility between the memory hierarchies of modern hardware accelerators and the mathematical requirements of standard sequence modeling paradigms. Contemporary sequence architectures, predominantly derived from the Transformer model, exhibit pathological memory bloat and experience catastrophic throughput degradation when tasked with processing millions of tokens. 

This systemic degradation stems inherently from the linear scaling of the required Key-Value (KV) cache memory footprint, coupled with the quadratic computational complexity inherent to dense token-to-token associative attention mechanisms. In this paper, we propose, define, and empirically evaluate a radical architectural departure: a reversible, block-wise intelligence substrate engineered exclusively for deterministic, perfectly flat scaling on graphical processing units (GPUs). By completely decoupling the dynamic memory footprint from the global sequence length and leveraging fixed-topology parallel reduction primitives, the proposed substrate maintains a strict memory complexity relative to the context size. 

The primary contribution of this research is the presentation of empirical results demonstrating highly stable, deterministic GPU throughput at unprecedented sequence lengths without revealing proprietary implementation details or core algorithmic update rules. In rigorously controlled evaluations, the substrate achieves a 131.75× operational speedup over optimized sequential CPU baselines at a 100-million-token sequence length, completing execution in exactly 0.0126 seconds. Furthermore, in a sustained 10-billion-token continuous streaming pass, the architecture maintains an entirely flat scaling profile, yielding an effective throughput exceeding 9.51 billion tokens per second. These results confirm that hardware-aligned reversible architectures can completely bypass the memory-bandwidth bottlenecks inherent to standard attention models, offering a scalable foundation for extreme-context sequence processing without algorithmic throughput degradation or non-deterministic statistical divergence.

title: The Effect of Correlation and Payoff Interdependence on Learning
affiliations: National Research University Higher School of Economics (Moscow) - International College of Economics and Finance and City, University of London

detail.title: The Effect of Correlation and Payoff Interdependence on Learning
detail.abstract: A firm chooses whether to invest in one of two projects. Projects' values are correlated and initially unknown. The firm can dynamically learn the values through investigating the projects either in parallel or sequentially. An increase in either correlation or interdependence of project values leads to a reduction in the optimal cumulative research effort but does not affect the allocation of learning resources whenever the firm investigates the projects in parallel.

title: What Level of Financial Inclusion Should Be Achieved? That is the Question
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: What Level of Financial Inclusion Should Be Achieved? That is the Question

publicationDetails.detailsText: Building Inclusive and Resilient Financial Ecosystems in the Digital Age, Springer.

detail.abstract: The level of financial inclusion is a measure of progress in development and policymakers are interested in knowing appropriate level of financial inclusion to attain. This article explores the question "what level of financial inclusion should be achieved?" Two alternative levels of financial inclusion are proposed. Financial inclusion policymakers should either focus on attaining the highest level of financial inclusion that is attainable, or they should focus on attaining an optimal level of financial inclusion. The article presents these two alternatives and argues in favour of attaining an optimal level of financial inclusion, which is the level of financial inclusion where the demand for financial services is equal to the supply of financial services. This optimal level of financial inclusion produces an equilibrium price at which financial service providers are willing to offer financial services on a continual basis and the price at which members of the population are willing to pay to access available financial services. Although a universal answer could not be provided to the question of which exact level of financial inclusion should be achieved, policymakers are advised to carefully determine the appropriate level of financial inclusion to achieve and choose a level of financial inclusion that helps to meet their economic and social objectives.

title: The Cost of Biological and Physical Distress: Testing the Farmer Health Capital Theory in India
affiliations: Maharashtra Agriculture Price Commission

detail.title: The Cost of Biological and Physical Distress: Testing the Farmer Health Capital Theory in India
detail.abstract: This paper advances the Farmer Health Capital (FHC) theory by empirically operationalising physical, mental, and social well-being as a composite, measurable productive input within the agricultural production function for sugarcane cultivation. Drawing on primary survey data from 150 smallholder farmers across Daund Taluka, Pune District, Maharashtra, we construct a multidimensional FHC Index and examine its relationship with agronomic and economic outcomes through Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression, binary logistic regression, Spearman rank-order correlations, chi-square tests of independence, and descriptive distributional analysis. The findings reveal a structurally distressed farming population: 96 per cent of farmers do not receive payment in a timely manner, 100 per cent reported crop loss in the survey year, 92 per cent skip meals during financial stress, 98 per cent lack access to clean drinking water in the field, 100 per cent lack pension or social security coverage, and 92 per cent experience treatment delays due to cost. Out-of-pocket (OOP) health expenditure averages 10.1 per cent of seasonal revenue, with 60 per cent borrowing for medical emergencies at informal rates. The logit regression establishes that the physical dimension of FHC is the single statistically significant predictor of farmer confidence in future agricultural seasons (odds ratio = 1.035; p < 0.001). The absence of a bioeconomy policy frameworkencompassing cooperative health insurance, nutritional supplementation, occupational safety, and technology diffusion-exacerbates these health deficits, constituting a structural failure with measurable output and welfare consequences. Finally, we advance actionable policy recommendations spanning cooperative health insurance, seasonal nutritional programs, and farm price-setting reforms.

title: The Rohingya Boat People in Indonesia's Territorial Waters: Navigating the Dilemma between Sovereignty, Humanitarianism, and Maritime Security
affiliations: Indonesia Defense University, Indonesia Defense University and Indonesia Defense University

detail.title: The Rohingya Boat People in Indonesia's Territorial Waters: Navigating the Dilemma between Sovereignty, Humanitarianism, and Maritime Security

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No known competing financial interests or personal relationships

detail.abstract: The arrival of Rohingya boat people in Indonesia's territorial waters presents a complex challenge involving state sovereignty, humanitarian obligations, and maritime security. Recurrent refugee movements, particularly in Aceh, affect maritime law enforcement, security stability, and Indonesia's political responsibility amid the absence of a comprehensive refugee framework. This article examines Indonesia's policy dilemma through the perspectives of maritime sovereignty, international maritime law, and nontraditional maritime security. Using a qualitative library research approach and a transdisciplinary perspective, the study analyzes international legal instruments, national regulations, reports from international organizations, and scientific literature on forced migration and maritime security. The findings show that Indonesia's response remains pragmatic and reactive, emphasizing humanitarian considerations without integration into national maritime defense and security strategies. This condition creates policy ambiguity that may weaken sovereignty enforcement, increase vulnerabilities in territorial waters, and create opportunities for organized transnational crime. The article argues that the Rohingya boat people issue should be understood not only as a humanitarian concern but also as a sovereignty and strategic maritime security challenge. Therefore, Indonesia requires a comprehensive, cross sectoral policy framework integrating legal, humanitarian, and maritime defense dimensions to strengthen sustainable maritime security governance in addressing regional forced migration dynamics and challenges effectively.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes HI-CODE (Human-Intent Coding), an intention-first framework for programming education in the generative AI era. Building on the author's previous work on AI ontology and Personal Sovereign AI, the paper argues that traditional syntax-first pedagogy increasingly trains students for tasks that generative AI can already perform efficiently, while neglecting higher-order capacities such as architectural thinking, system design, judgment, and creative problem-solving. HI-CODE introduces a three-stage Scaffolded Release Model: Dribbling, in which students use AI to build complete products through framework selection and PRD-driven development; Shooting, in which students evaluate, refine, and coordinate AI-generated systems; and Tactics, in which students study syntax and underlying principles through reverse reconstruction and deeper technical analysis. Syntax is treated as an important but secondary layer of understanding that emerges from prior product experience. A distinctive feature of the framework is the integration of programming aesthetics into the curriculum. Through structured activities in system aesthetics, mind aesthetics, and expression aesthetics, students develop the capacity to evaluate elegance, coherence, simplicity, and human-centered design. The paper further outlines five proposed methodologies for empirical validation and argues that programming education should shift from code production toward architectural intention and human-AI collaboration. HI-CODE is presented as a conceptual foundation for cultivating pedagogical sovereignty and preparing students for a future in which AI increasingly automates routine programming tasks.

title: A Bee in the Bundeskartellamt's Bonnet: Amazon Fined for its Price Control Mechanisms
affiliations: University Villanueva

detail.title: A Bee in the Bundeskartellamt's Bonnet: Amazon Fined for its Price Control Mechanisms
detail.abstract: In February 2025, Germany's Bundeskartellamt fined Amazon €59 million for its price control mechanisms on the German marketplace, finding these to constitute an abuse of dominance under Section 19a(2) GWB, Section 19 GWB, and Article 102 TFEU. Amazon's algorithmic pricing tools penalise third-party sellers whose prices are deemed erroneous, excessive, or uncompetitive by removing their offers or suppressing their visibility in the Featured Offer. The authority argues these practices distort downstream competition, particularly harming small and medium-sized sellers unable to cover their costs under Amazon's imposed price thresholds. This article critically examines the FCO's theory of harm, questioning its consumer welfare rationale, and highlights the procedural complexity arising from the case's overlap with Article 5(3) of the Digital Markets Act. It further raises concerns about fragmented enforcement across EU Member States and the European Commission's decision not to pursue a harmonised remedy.

title: All for One, and One for None: The European Commission's Implementation Measures Target New Entries in the AI Assistant Market
affiliations: University Villanueva

detail.title: All for One, and One for None: The European Commission's Implementation Measures Target New Entries in the AI Assistant Market
detail.abstract: In April 2025, the European Commission published draft implementation measures under Article 6(7) of the Digital Markets Act, requiring Google to open four layers of its Android operating system to third-party AI competitors: invocation, contextual data access, app and OS actions, and device resource allocation. Unlike prior specification proceedings against Apple, which addressed non-compliance, these measures are anticipatory, insofar as they seek to preserve contestability in AI-driven smartphone markets before dominance consolidates. The measures mandate equal-effectiveness interoperability across nine Android features, covering assistants, hotword detection, sensor access, and background execution, all free of charge. However, the draft measures exhibit notable limitations: quantitative performance benchmarks are largely absent, hardware constraints on DSPs and NPUs are inadequately addressed, cloud infrastructure is omitted entirely, and OEM fragmentation risks undermine uniform implementation. The article concludes that, despite the Commission's ambition, technical and enforcement gaps may render the measures ineffective in practice.

title: Inside of Structural Economy: An Approach from Informal Angola Economy

detail.abstract: This approach focuses specifically on the behaviour of the economy, that is, its economic structure, with particular emphasis on the formal and informal sectors. Thus, the evidence points specifically to the plausible existence of an informal economy in Angola, the significance of which is in fact closely linked to the very nature of the determining factors that are, by their very nature, relevant. A key feature of the informal economic structure relates, above all, to the fact that there is, for example, a limited capacity on the part of the state to generate wealth, as evidenced by significant tax losses; for instance, Angola incurs an annual tax loss of 6.9 billion dollars. On the other hand, however, it nevertheless represents a significant opportunity cost in terms of public policy; thus, the analysis suggests that, to the extent that there is a substantial expansion of the informal economy, on the other hand, there is a particular trend towards the continuous emergence of new informal professions. Informal markets exhibit characteristics that are specific to them; for example, most informal workers do not have fixed monthly incomes, and income levels depend directly on daily informal economic activities. Thus, the greater the flow of informal economic activities, the higher the income levels of economic agents will naturally be. On the other hand, approach show in particular, that, many Underdevelopment Countries, they not give attention to informal economy, where, on majority of this countries see the informal economy as statistics, the politics and institutions not exist in these Countries, in particular.

title: The Chicken or Egg Dilemma: The General Court Partially Annuls the European Commission's DMA Designation Decision Against Meta (Case T-1078/23)
affiliations: University Villanueva

detail.title: The Chicken or Egg Dilemma: The General Court Partially Annuls the European Commission's DMA Designation Decision Against Meta (Case T-1078/23)
detail.abstract: In its June 2026 ruling on Meta's designation under the Digital Markets Act, the General Court largely upheld the European Commission's findings regarding Facebook Messenger while partially annulling the designation of Facebook Marketplace. With respect to Messenger, the court confirmed its delineation as a separate core platform service from Facebook and its characterisation as a number-independent interpersonal communications service, relying on a cluster of recurring arguments that simultaneously served to justify delineation, categorisation, and rebuttal rejection. This circular reasoning resurfaces the chicken-and-egg dilemma previously identified in ByteDance v Commission, leaving the legal standard for rebutting gatekeeper designations unresolved. Regarding Facebook Marketplace, the court annulled the designation for the Commission's failure to adequately account for material factual changes occurring before the designation decision was finalised. The ruling raises significant questions about the temporal scope of designation assessments, the probative burden on gatekeepers, and the practical consequences of ex tunc annulment where compliance measures have already been implemented.

title: Lobbying to Decouple
affiliations: University of Bath - School of Management, ALBA Graduate Business School, Durham Business School, City University London - Faculty of Management and Western University

detail.title: Lobbying to Decouple
detail.abstract: Why do firms so often fail to deliver on, or backslide from, their climate commitments? We argue that political lobbying buffers decoupling from external scrutiny, allowing firms to sustain a gap between their public commitments and their actual environmental performance. Firms invest in political influence to blunt the accountability and delay the policy and oversight pressure, preserving ambitious public commitments without fulfilling their climate targets. Using three measures of climate target attainment, including a novel text-based measure of derived from earnings-call disclosures, we find that lobbying intensity predicts lower target achievement. Employing stacked difference-indifferences across seventeen exogenous state-level policy shocks, we find that the lobbyingdecoupling relationship strengthens when firms face targeted new environmental policies that political influence can directly counter. By contrast, it weakens under Democratic administrations, when accountability pressure is more demanding, consistent with strategic rather than habitual political engagement. Institutional ownership works against this relationship, offsetting part of the decoupling that lobbying drives. These findings extend decoupling theory by identifying political lobbying as the mechanism through which firms convert institutional pressure into political protection, sustaining the gap between climate commitment and environmental performance.

title: Managing Human-Bear Conflict in Trentino, Italy: Policy Options for Coexistence

detail.title: Managing Human-Bear Conflict in Trentino, Italy: Policy Options for Coexistence
detail.abstract:
The reintroduction of brown bears (Ursus arctos) in Trentino, Northern Italy, supported by the EU LIFE Ursus Programme (1999-2004), represents one of the most emblematic initiatives for wildlife conservation in Europe. It has been associated with positive outcomes for the alpine ecosystems, and significant socio-economic benefits. Nevertheless, the bear population recovery has also contributed to the re-emergence of human-bear conflicts, a phenomenon which is especially severe in highly anthropized valleys. In recent years, reported encounters, including attacks, have grown in frequency, alongside rising economic costs and legal disputes, accompanied by a decline in public trust towards environmental governance.

 

This policy report aims to address the question of how the Autonomous Province of Trento (APT) should respond to these challenges, and how it can support coexistence by mitigating the conflict without undermining the compliance with the EU Habitats Directive and national regulations, while safeguarding conservation objectives in the long-term. 

 

Adopting a qualitative policy analysis framework, I identify key drivers of conflict and evaluate three policy options: maintaining the status quo through the continuation of an annual culling quota (A); regulating access to at-risk zones (B); and extending regulated access to bear deterrent spray (C).

For conducting the assessment of these alternatives, I consider, for their relevance, five key dimensions: equity in the distribution of benefits and costs, conservation outcomes, legal and regulatory compliance, economic efficiency, and political feasibility. Option C emerges as the most balanced pathway for addressing the trade-offs between safety, conservation and practicability. The results call for further reflection on the potential of non-lethal deterrence strategies in promoting human-wildlife coexistence in densely populated areas, which necessitate, as a fundamental prerequisite for their effective implementation, reinforced educational and monitoring frameworks.

title:
Latent-State Theory of Risk and Ambiguity Preferences: 
Foundations, Limiting Cases, and Practical Illustrations

detail.title:
Latent-State Theory of Risk and Ambiguity Preferences: 
Foundations, Limiting Cases, and Practical Illustrations
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a new theoretical framework, called the Latent-State Theory of Risk and Ambiguity Preferences. The central idea is that observed preferences under risk and ambiguity are not only revealed by choices, but are formed conditionally on a latent decision state. This state may capture reference points, perceived ruin, trust, stress, comparative ignorance, social evaluation, model uncertainty, time pressure, and the mode of elicitation. The framework introduces state-conditional preferences and shows that expected utility theory, Arrow-Pratt risk aversion, higher-order risk preferences, maxmin expected utility, smooth ambiguity, and cumulative prospect theory can be recovered as limiting or restricted cases. The paper develops a set of foundational axioms, derives representation results, and proposes several propositions linking latent states to dynamic risk aversion, prudence, temperance, ambiguity aversion, probability weighting, and preference reversals. Practical illustrations are provided through managerial risk taking, Ellsberg-type ambiguity, three-outcome ambiguity, insurance under nonperformance risk, international portfolio underdiversification, incentive contracting, and public decision-making under catastrophic uncertainty.

detail.abstract:
The Western Hemisphere contains approximately 1.2 billion people, rapidly expanding technology sectors, extraordinary linguistic diversity, and a long tradition of multilateral cooperation through institutions including the Organization of American States, the Inter-American Development Bank, and the Corporacion Andina de Fomento. It lacks, however, the permanent institutional infrastructure required to govern artificial intelligence at a regional scale. This paper argues that this absence constitutes a structural failure with compounding consequences: absent shared standards, shared compute access, and durable governance norms, the Americas will remain consumers rather than architects of transformative AI technology, and the governance frameworks that shape how AI systems work will continue to be designed without systematic input from the majority of the hemisphere's population.

We propose GLAPAGOS, the Global Laboratory for AI Progress and Governance: Open Systems, as a framework for addressing this gap. Drawing on the institutional design of CERN as an analytic model, the paper articulates the conditions under which a multilateral open AI platform can function effectively across a politically heterogeneous region, the governance architecture required to sustain such a platform over time, and the policy mechanisms through which participating nations and institutions can align incentives without surrendering national distinctiveness. We situate GLAPAGOS within the existing landscape of regional AI governance, including the Santiago Declaration of 2023, the Ibero-American Charter for AI in Public Administration, H.Res. 649 of the 118th U.S. Congress, and the IDB regulatory framework for AI in Latin America and the Caribbean. We conclude that the hemisphere does not lack the political will to cooperate on artificial intelligence; it lacks the institutional substrate through which that will can be made technically coherent, permanently available, and democratically accountable.

title: The Architect's Mandate: Leading Through Orchestration

detail.title: The Architect's Mandate: Leading Through Orchestration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently.

detail.abstract:
The era of the 'charismatic visionary' NGO leader — the centralized savior-figure who controls every decision-making loop — is no longer merely obsolete. It is a direct operational liability. In a complex humanitarian ecosystem where a single mission may span multiple volatile political environments under active state surveillance, centralized management chains produce Decision Bottleneck Friction (Fb) that systematically exceeds 1.0 — meaning administrative latency is slower than threat velocity. The result is predictable: project failures, asset losses, staff endangerment, and institutional paralysis at precisely the moments of maximum operational demand.

This paper introduces the framework of Orchestration and Distributed Autonomy, drawing from the Prussian military doctrine of Auftragstaktik (Mission-Type Tactics) — formalized by von Moltke the Elder between 1857 and 1871 — and from the operational precedent of Admiral Nelson's 'Band of Brothers' command philosophy at the Battle of Trafalgar (1805). We introduce three original quantitative instruments: the Decision Bottleneck Friction formula (Fb), which measures administrative latency against threat velocity; the Decentralized Decision Ratio (Dr), which quantifies an organization's actual autonomy architecture; and the Institutional Muscle Memory Index (IMM), which measures whether distributed autonomy has been genuinely internalized or merely declared.

We demonstrate that the structural requirements for Orchestrated leadership are inseparable from the financial sovereignty framework introduced in Essay 2 (FAI ≥ 0.6) and the distributed resilience architecture of Essay 3 (Ωip < 2.0, γ_redundancy → 1.0). An organization that cannot fund its own operations independently cannot grant genuine autonomy to its field cells. An organization that has not built local organizational capacity cannot survive the leadership transitions that high-autonomy systems require. The three essays form a structural trilogy: financial sovereignty enables organizational autonomy; organizational autonomy enables distributed resilience; distributed resilience enables mission survival in multi-polar environments.

We conclude by introducing The 30-Day Shadow Autonomy Test as the definitive diagnostic for organizational readiness: if an organization's executive headquarters goes offline for 30 consecutive days, can the frontline network continue to perform, adapt, and innovate at full operational capacity — guided entirely by institutional muscle memory and pre-defined strategic intent? Any answer other than 'yes' is a structural failure that must be corrected before the next operational crisis makes it irrelevant.

title: Sport as a Meaning-Production Industry: Bounded-Risk Simulation, Narrative Capital, and an A-N-I Model with Institutional Gating

detail.title: Sport as a Meaning-Production Industry: Bounded-Risk Simulation, Narrative Capital, and an A-N-I Model with Institutional Gating

detail.abstract: This paper treats sport as a meaning-production industry: a bounded-risk simulation that converts uncertainty, under trusted rules, into shareable interpretation and priceable value. It develops a minimal AN -I model in which exposure (A), narrative intensity (N), and identity payload (I) generate monetizable value only through an institutional reliability gate g(R). Narrative intensity is decomposed as N = N_eng × S, distinguishing engagement density from scarcity and cycle. The framework connects primitive unbounded-risk settings such as solo hunting and gambling to modern sport by showing how rules, officiating, calendars, and governance transform raw uncertainty into repeatable narrative capital. The paper also specifies failure modes with observable signatures: integrity shocks lower R and can trigger moral exit; betting-driven demeaning substitutes probability discourse for narrative discourse; and short-form fragmentation raises exposure while weakening arc continuity, completion, and cross-event linkage. The result is a cultural-economy account of sport as a valuation technology rather than merely a leisure market or media-rights business. It reframes the classic uncertainty-of-outcome hypothesis as trust-conditional: outcome uncertainty creates cultural-economic value only when audiences can interpret it as legitimate suspense rather than manipulation.

title: Trends and Structural Shifts in Blood Product Wastage at a Chinese Regional Blood Center, 2019–2025: A Seven-Year Retrospective Time-Series Analysis

detail.title: Trends and Structural Shifts in Blood Product Wastage at a Chinese Regional Blood Center, 2019–2025: A Seven-Year Retrospective Time-Series Analysis
detail.abstract: Background: Blood product wastage reduces the usable supply of a limited therapeutic resource and is a key quality indicator for blood establishments. Longitudinal, cause-specific data from Chinese blood centers remain limited, particularly for lipemia-related plasma discard.Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 84 months of aggregate discard data from January 2019 to December 2025 at a regional blood center in China. Discard causes were grouped into seven major and 24 minor categories. Overall and component-specific discard rates were summarized, and interrupted time-series models with Fourier seasonal terms and Newey–West standard errors assessed the association between the sustained COVID-19 containment period and discard rates.Results: Among 2,504,680 three-component products prepared from 1,086,357 whole-blood donations, 122,099 units were discarded, yielding a weighted mean monitoring discard rate of 4.87%. The annual rate decreased from 6.19% in 2019 to 2.81% in 2022, rebounded to 6.36% in 2024, and declined to 4.18% in 2025. Lipemia was the leading cause in five of seven years and accounted for most variation in plasma and overall discard rates. The COVID-19 containment period was associated with a 2.05-percentage-point reduction in the overall discard rate (β = −2.047; 95% CI, −3.055 to −1.039; p < 0.001), concentrated in plasma lipemia. Preparation defects decreased, whereas volume non-conformity increased.Conclusions: Plasma lipemia was the principal driver of discard-rate variation. Component- and subtype-level monitoring can identify actionable signals for wastage-reduction programs.

title: A Sequential Regime Framework for U.S. Equity Drawdown Periods: Integration of Two Empirical Classifications and Distribution-Free Validation via Conformal Prediction

detail.title: A Sequential Regime Framework for U.S. Equity Drawdown Periods: Integration of Two Empirical Classifications and Distribution-Free Validation via Conformal Prediction
detail.abstract:
This paper integrates two empirical regime classifications from the author's series — the HABITUATED regime (Takagi, 2026a) and the HIGH-DOWN regime of a macro fear score (Takagi, 2026b) — into a unified three-phase framework for U.S. equity drawdown periods.

Across the S&P 500 sample (January 1990 to April 2026, 9,117 trading days), the two regimes are near-disjoint at the daily resolution yet sequentially linked: every one of the ten HABITUATED episode end-points is followed by a HIGH-DOWN activation. This motivates a three-phase classification — Phase I (HABITUATED), Phase II (Healing Period), Phase III (Recovery) — whose conditional 250-day forward-return distributions are sharply distinct, with non-overlapping bootstrap intervals between Phase I (mean -21.2%) and Phase III (mean +22.9%).

We validate the conditional intervals with split conformal prediction and examine their robustness, including the limits of out-of-episode generalisation. The framework is descriptive throughout: it characterises conditional return distributions and proposes no forecast or trading rule. The structure rests on two historical episodes (the dot-com collapse and the global financial crisis), and we are explicit about the scope this implies.

detail.abstract: Customer Support practitioners perform demanding relational and communicative work under a structural condition that no existing occupational framework has formally named or measured. Asymmetric face exposure (AFE) is that condition: the structural state in which a professional role simultaneously maximizes face-threatening exposure and institutionally prohibits the face-protective communicative responses that would be available to any social actor in an equivalent interpersonal situation. Face theory establishes the bilateral access to face-protective response that standard social interaction presupposes; the Conversation Analysis literature on institutional talk establishes that professional roles constrain that access; neither framework, nor their combination, addresses the occupational cost of systematic prohibition encoded in role architecture rather than in individual interactions or organizational dysfunction. This paper makes four theoretical contributions. First, it formally derives and develops the asymmetric face exposure construct from the intersection of face theory, institutional talk research, and occupational sociology, demonstrating a gap that none of those frameworks individually or in combination has previously reached. Second, it develops two analytically distinct prohibition mechanisms-Type 1 explicit prohibition, which preserves a partial performer/performance identity separation, and Type 2 normative prohibition, which absorbs the constraint into the practitioner's own professional self-concept and generates second-order normalization. Third, it introduces attribution prohibition as a specific Type 1 variant: the structural requirement to absorb causal responsibility for outcomes generated by other organizational functions under institutional prohibition of accurate attribution. Fourth, it introduces empathic exposure as a distinct harm pathway, demonstrating that genuine attunement rather than hostile face attack can be the source of harm accumulation, and that practitioner excellence and harm accumulation are, under current structural conditions, positively correlated. The moderating architecture, measurement instrument, and preliminary empirical evidence are developed in a companion paper currently in preparation.

detail.abstract:
This paper enumerates minimal winning coalitions in weighted voting games with unit weights, where an incompatibility graph restricts feasible coalitions to independent sets. We focus on two fundamental graph classes: the path \(P_n\) and the cycle \(C_n\). We first establish a general hereditary characterization, for any hereditary feasibility system and unit weights, a feasible coalition is minimal winning if and only if it contains exactly \(q\) players. Consequently, the enumeration problem reduces to counting independent sets of size \(q\).
For the path \(P_n\), we derive a recurrence for the number of independent sets of a given size and solve it to obtain the closed form \(\binom{n-q+1}{q}\). For the cycle \(C_n\), we condition on the inclusion of a fixed vertex to obtain \(\binom{n-q}{q} + \binom{n-q-1}{q-1}\). We complement these exact formulas with an asymptotic analysis for both fixed quotas and proportional quotas \(q = \alpha n\), derive exact expressions for the number of minimal winning coalitions containing a given player (a natural power index), and present generating functions that connect the enumeration to Fibonacci polynomials. For arbitrary integer weights, we develop a pseudo-polynomial dynamic programming algorithm to count the number of feasible coalitions. These closed-form formulas are computable in constant time, offering rare exact enumerations for graph-restricted voting games and bridging cooperative game theory with classical combinatorics.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the financial and non-financial trade-offs between private car ownership and ride-hailing services (Uber and PickMe) for urban commuters in Sri Lanka, a developing economy characterized by severely distorted vehicle prices due to import restrictions and taxation. Using a comparative case study design grounded in Multivism, the study analyzes two vehicle categories, moderate cars (LKR 10 million, e.g., Toyota Raize) and lower-grade cars (LKR 6 million, e.g., Suzuki Wagon R), against ride-hailing alternatives for a typical 40 km daily round trip (880 km monthly). Financial analysis incorporating lease payments, fuel, insurance, maintenance, and opportunity cost of down payment reveals that ride-hailing services (LKR 150/km for moderate segment; LKR 125/km for lower-grade) are cheaper than owning a moderate car (LKR 213/km) by LKR 63/km (LKR 55,500 monthly). However, the gap narrows substantially for lower-grade ownership (LKR 136/km), creating a marginal difference of LKR 14/km (LKR 9,500 monthly) against comparable ride-hailing options. The paper concludes that financial irrationality lies not in car ownership per se but in owning vehicles inappropriately expensive for one's actual mobility needs. Non-financial considerations, privacy, availability, family utility, and autonomy versus driving stress, coordination friction, and asset management burden, become decisive at narrow cost differentials.

title: A Firmer Footing for Cratics: Control as a Praxeological Category
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Firmer Footing for Cratics: Control as a Praxeological Category
detail.abstract: Rahim Taghizadegan and Marc-Felix Otto have opened a promising field of research with their article Praxeology of Coercion: Catallactics vs. Cratics (2015). Cratic action, or threat-based human action, seeks a non-market interpersonal exchange. The threat of violence makes such an exchange a negative analog to offer-based catallactic action. As both actions result in a type of exchange (an induced action by the recipient), the distinction between offer and threat takes central importance. Unfortunately, the authors' basis for distinction potentially undermines this new field of praxeology before it gets off the ground: (1) defining an offer as allowing rejection free of cost, and (2) distinguishing offer and threat by reference to a presupposed norm. This paper will argue that an alternative criterion, control of means, puts this new field on firmer scientific footing while avoiding these pitfalls. Because control of means is a praxeological category of every action, it can serve as the value-free criterion to distinguish offers from threats. The first part of this paper will briefly summarize cratics and present the problems with the authors' foundational distinction. The second section will establish control of means as an a priori praxeological category. The third section will apply control as an alternative criterion to the offer/threat distinction to resolve the problems presented in the first part. The final part will make some brief observations regarding light that the analysis of control can shed on certain puzzles.
