detail.title: Capitalism and Self-Referential Ignorance: A Systems-Theoretical Analysis Through the Universal Balance Feedback Framework (UBFF)
detail.abstract: Capitalism is one of the most consequential economic systems in human history, generating unprecedented advances in productivity, innovation, and aggregate wealth. Yet capitalist systems repeatedly generate crises, deepen inequality, produce corruption, and sustain speculative manias-often despite the presence of formal error-correction mechanisms. This paper proposes that these phenomena are systematically explained by Self-Referential Ignorance (SRI), a formally defined condition in which an agent, institution, or system increasingly validates its beliefs through internally generated assumptions rather than external corrective feedback. SRI is operationalized as a measurable index (SRI-I) derived from four observable dimensions: epistemic closure, feedback suppression, error persistence, and adaptive rigidity. Drawing on the Universal Balance Feedback Framework (UBFF)-whose master equation Wr = ∫(Is • Bu • FL • IN) • Dc governs systemic welfare as a function of integrity, balance, feedback, and nodal interconnection-this paper develops a formal dynamical model of SRI accumulation and systemic correction. Lyapunov stability analysis demonstrates that capitalist equilibria are conditionally stable and that SRI constitutes a destabilizing force whose magnitude is bounded by institutional feedback capacity. Historical cases including the Dot-Com bubble, the 2007-2009 Global Financial Crisis, and the organizational failures of Kodak and Nokia are examined as empirical instantiations of the SRI dynamic. Falsifiable predictions are derived from the model. The paper concludes that the long-term stability of capitalist systems depends not on profit maximization per se, but on the structural preservation of feedback integrity.

detail.abstract: The United States has achieved unparalleled technological acceleration over the past three decades, yet this acceleration rests on a physical substrate-electrical grids, transmission infrastructure, material supply chains-that has been systematically underfunded, abstractly rendered invisible, and ideologically subordinated to a techno-utopian faith in software-defined solutions. This paper argues that Western, and particularly American, techno-capitalism has replicated the structural logic of religious institutions: it posits an original sin of scarcity, promises salvation through emergent technologies such as artificial general intelligence (AGI) and fusion energy, canonizes venture-backed prophets who offer 18-month eschatological timelines, and heretically marginalises any voice that foregrounds material infrastructure. Drawing on historical sociology, political economy, philosophy of science, and complexity theory, the paper traces the ideological genealogy of this infrastructure blindness from Manifest Destiny through cloud-era abstraction layers. It models the anticipated consequences-grid fragmentation, social contract erosion, neo-Luddite reaction, and intra-industry schism-and benchmarks these dynamics against East Asian developmental state models that treat overprovisioning as actuarial insurance rather than waste. The paper concludes that the United States faces a Cartesian inflection point: it must relearn to doubt its physical assumptions before it can reconstruct a durable substrate for the technological futures it otherwise correctly imagines.

detail.title: Convergent Faults -A Quantitative Forensic of Private Credit Synchronized Systemic Risk (2026-2027)
detail.abstract:
Private credit has gone from roughly $400 billion in 2009 to about $3 trillion in mid-2026. U.S. business development companies (BDCs) now hold close to half a trillion of that, split across three architectures with very different liquidity and disclosure properties. The official line, repeated by the Federal Reserve, the Financial Stability Board and most sell-side credit desks, calls the resulting risk "limited and manageable." Fund-level leverage is low, defaults are below the long-run leveraged-loan average, and bank exposure looks bounded. We argue that the official line works only when each stress channel is examined alone, and breaks down once the channels are read together. 

This paper documents five channels: software and SaaS valuation compression under AI disruption; bank-to-non-bank credit tightening, with JPMorgan as first mover; retail liquidity gating at perpetual non-traded BDCs; the "Bermuda Triangle" of related-party lending between Apollo and Athene, KKR and Global Atlantic, Brookfield and its affiliated insurers; and the 2026-2027 refinancing wall hitting a sector that has just lost its bid. Using Bloomberg Intelligence proprietary research, regulatory data and the public filings of the largest BDCs, we show that these channels are coupled. Each one tightens the others under plausible macroeconomic conditions, and the joint stress horizon is short enough to read on a calendar. 

The cascade is already visible. On 4 June 2026 Blackstone Private Credit Fund, the largest BDC, $82.1 billion of holdings, gated quarterly redemptions at 5% of NAV against requests of 10%. Its $1 billion 6% 2032 notes trade 150 basis points wide of triple-B financial peers, against an adviser (Blackstone Inc.) rated A+/A+. We map the catalysts that lie ahead, assign probabilities to three outcome scenarios, and identify a convergence window centred on Q1-Q2 2027.

title: Anger Genome Model: How Anger, Threat, Guilt, and Control Encode Toxic Workplace Cultures
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Anger Genome Model: How Anger, Threat, Guilt, and Control Encode Toxic Workplace Cultures
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes the Anger Genome Model, a socio-ecological genetic framework for understanding toxic workplace cultures as recurrent emotional and organizational sequences. The term “genome” is used metaphorically, not biologically, to describe how repeated patterns of Anger, Threat, Guilt, and Control encode harmful workplace cultures. In this model, A represents Anger, T represents Threat, G represents Guilt, and C represents Control.

The central argument is that toxic workplace cultures are not produced merely by angry supervisors, individual emotional dysregulation, or isolated harassment incidents. Rather, they emerge when anger, threat, guilt, and control are connected in specific sequences and repeatedly enacted within organizational environments. For example, an A→T→G→C sequence begins with anger, which becomes threat, produces guilt, and eventually enables control. By contrast, a C→A→T→G sequence begins with control, often appearing at first as instruction, support, or careful guidance. When the controlled person deviates from expected conduct, anger emerges, repeated anger becomes threat, and threat eventually produces guilt, such as the feeling that one is unsuitable for the workplace.

Drawing on research on abusive supervision, petty tyranny, workplace bullying, psychological safety, organizational silence, emotional contagion, institutional theory, cultural evolution, and meme theory, this paper redefines workplace harassment as a patterned emotional sequence rather than a single act or individual personality problem. It also discusses mutation and transcription within anger genomes. When overt anger becomes difficult to express, it may mutate into silence, information blocking, exclusion, or formalized control. Similarly, interpersonal anger-based control may be transcribed into organizational procedures such as written warnings, demands for reflection, disciplinary processes, and symbolic sanctions.

The paper argues that effective harassment prevention requires reading and interrupting the entire emotional sequence, not merely suppressing visible anger. Organizations must examine how anger connects to threat, how threat produces guilt, how guilt enables control, and how these patterns are reproduced, institutionalized, and transformed. The Anger Genome Model thus offers a diagnostic and theoretical framework for analyzing toxic workplace cultures, recurrence of harassment, organizational silence, turnover, and the failure of preventive duties.

detail.title: Central Asia's Capacity to Study China and Contribute to Policy-making
detail.abstract: This article examines Central Asia's capacity to study China and produce policy-relevant knowledge about its increasingly important neighbour. Drawing on oral history interviews with three "giants" of Central Asian Sinology-Klara Khafizova and Konstantin Syroezhkin of Kazakhstan and Abdul-Ahad Ablat Khodjaev of Uzbekistan-alongside published scholarship, think tank reports, and informal consultations with contemporary researchers, the article identifies a paradox: as economic and political ties between Central Asian states and China deepen, indigenous capacity for independent, rigorous China analysis is diminishing. The three scholars are treated not as representatives of the field as a whole, but as a historical baseline demonstrating what rigorous, institutionally embedded China expertise once looked like-and against which the current capacity gap can be measured. Three interconnected dimensions of challenge are diagnosed-educational, state, and public-each rooted in the collapse of the Soviet Sinological tradition and exacerbated by institutional fragility, limited political will, and a polarised public discourse. The article concludes with an actionable blueprint for strengthening regional capacity, centred on foundational educational reform, professional community-building, and joint international research cooperation, with explicit attention to the structural barriers each recommendation must overcome.

title: Capabilities Analysis in Competition Policy: Evidence from Merger Remedies
affiliations: European University Institute - Department of Law (LAW) and European University Institute - Department of Law (LAW)

detail.title: Capabilities Analysis in Competition Policy: Evidence from Merger Remedies
detail.abstract: The business and strategic management literature shows that dynamic competition depends on firm-level capabilities. Yet, firm-level capabilities do not feature in the variables used in the economic evaluation of mergers. For that reason, integrating capabilities analysis in merger policy is often perceived as a challenge. This paper questions that perception. We examine whether competition agencies already conduct capabilities analyses in merger enforcement, focusing on purchaser approval decisions following divestiture orders. Using a unique dataset of 109 such decisions adopted by the European Commission between 2014 and 2025, we find that the Commission conducts some capability analysis in two-thirds of cases, with thorough examinations occurring in one-third. The intensity of this analysis varies substantially by industry: it is high in pharmaceuticals and chemicals but low or absent in basic metals, electrical equipment, and retail. When capabilities are analyzed, the Commission focuses overwhelmingly on post-merger integration capabilities, with other capabilities like R&D and scaling receiving comparatively less attention. Furthermore, the Commission rarely rejects proposed purchasers on capability grounds. The results hold across the entire relevant period. We discuss the implications for merger remedy design and dynamic competition policy.

title: Structuring Collaboration Memory for AI-Augmented Negotiation: A Practitioner Methodology for Persistent Human-AI Partnership
affiliations: Catholic University of Milan - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Structuring Collaboration Memory for AI-Augmented Negotiation: A Practitioner Methodology for Persistent Human-AI Partnership
detail.abstract: Negotiation practitioners increasingly prepare cases and draft strategies alongside AI systems, and much recent work has gone into stopping such a system from beginning each session blank. But giving an AI a memory of facts is not the same as giving a partnership a memory of itself. Working with an AI over months is not a string of sessions that happen to share a memory; it is a collaboration that can improve-yet what a practitioner and an AI learn about working together (which decisions were settled and which rejected, how the practitioner reasons and wants to be challenged, how the two divide the labor and learn from each other) is lost by default, because the AI retains nothing between sessions and the practitioner does not reliably carry what was settled or where the work last stood. I call this distance the collaboration memory gap, and argue that it can be closed deliberately, in plain text files that record and curate the collaboration itself. Drawing on a single sustained case-a memory system built and refined across my own negotiation projects-I show that such a record has four layers (the work, the working style, the thinking partnership, and the learning) and that, kept and curated, it makes the partnership compound rather than merely persist: practitioner and AI come to produce together what neither would alone. From the practice I draw four transferable ideas-the shared mind, collaboration memory, synergy, and "borrow structure, not infrastructure"-and ask how far they reach beyond negotiation. The contribution is a methodology, not a tool: a replicable way of structuring a human-AI partnership so that, in the worked case of negotiation, an augmented negotiator gets better every day.

detail.abstract: Vision document • green paper • deliberately non-final, written to be outgrown Amended edition (v2) • introducing the Fourth Sovereign Substrate: The Sovereign Home What this is. A companion to the Model Law and its papers, written in a different key. The Model Law is an instrument; this is a horizon. It does not propose rules but possibilities-ways in which the ideas now gathered around the REIVJ project (the honest coupling of causal and probabilistic reasoning; the smart contract recast as a contestable fact; sovereign hardware and off-grid intelligence; a sovereign, rights-protective dwelling; a democratized Internet of Things; and a reciprocal, non-extractive economy of contribution) might, step by step and only as they prove themselves, let every willing and capable legal subject take part in a scientifictechnological evolution. An evolution which would be capable of delegitimizing many of the catastrophizing, even apocalyptic, negatively deterministic vocabulary about technological developments being followed by a regression of humankind. Such views are manifestations of conative imbalances. What this amended edition adds. The first edition described three sovereign substrates-a door the participant owns, a mind the participant owns, and a shared discipline of reasoning. This edition adds the fourth, without which the first three are exercised in an exposed and permeable space: the Sovereign Home-the physically and electromagnetically inviolable dwelling within which a sovereign person may rest, recover, reason and contribute, and at whose boundary the inhabitant-not the ambient technological environment-decides what enters and what does not. The addition of the fourth substrate also enlarges the vision of who the Network is for: not only institutes, but every willing and capable person who, now actually possessing these four sovereignties, wishes to take part in the refinement of any body of knowledge. Finally, this edition makes explicit, in a new Part H, the threefold yield of realizing the framework: a wider and more effective realization of fundamental rights beyond the two that anchor the substrates; new sources of scientific contribution; and new livelihoods in the production of the substrates' physical components-three classes of benefit that reinforce one another in a virtuous circle. This is a vision document, not a version of the Model Law. It states no binding rule and closes nothing. In keeping with the request that animates it, and with Principle VII of Version 5.0, it is written to be superseded: each future version of the model is to be treated as a molt rather than a final form.

detail.title: Switching at the Warranted Rate: Distributive Cycles as a Boundary-Equilibrium Bifurcation (companion to "Same-Gap Coupling and the (Im)possibility of Endogenous Distributive Cycles")
detail.abstract: In a companion paper [1] we characterised, for smooth C 1 accumulation-distribution systems, which Harrodian-Cambridge closures can host endogenous distributive cycles, the discriminating invariant being sgn det DF (x *) at a gap-closing equilibrium; the constructive model there-Model C-has a supercritical Hopf in the profit-squeeze strength φ u , with amplitude growing as φ u-φ H u. This paper observes that Model C's equilibrium sits exactly on the warranted-rate surface Σ = {g = 0}, and asks what happens when the accumulation response kinks there, η → η ± , as irreversibility-plus-aggregation makes it. The same equilibrium then hosts a second bifurcation-a non-smooth boundary-focuswhose amplitude grows linearly in its unfolding; the √ •-versus-linear contrast discriminates the two mechanisms in the same calibrated model. We borrow the gap, anchor, Model C and the determinant invariant from [1] and do not re-derive them. The structural backbone is the boundary-equilibrium bifurcation (BEB): the regional Jacobians A ± = A 0 + η ± bc ⊤ and the determinant collapse det A ± = det A 0 (1 + η ± µ) are the classification of di Bernardo-Nordmark-Olivar (DNO, [6]), and the planar criterion Λ = σ + /ω + + σ-/ω-is their Thm. 5.1. On this backbone we obtain a sharp three-part answer on the calibrated 3D Model C. (R1, negative) A pure accumulation kink with the gap orthogonal to the response direction (c ⊤ b = 0) and the equilibrium pinned to Σ is nondestabilising: although the planar cone exponent Λ does cross zero (at ∆η c ≈ 0.774), the regime-invariant trace forces the spiral repulsion to be paid for by an exactly compensating strengthening of the contracting real direction, and the full-dimensional return multiplier µ ret (∆η) < 1 throughout the smoothly stable regime and decreases in ∆η. Planar Λ > 0 is necessary but not sufficient. (R2, negative) A switch placed symmetrically on the distributive gap leaves the time-averaged trace pinned at-ω and likewise cannot destabilise. (R3, positive) The cycle requires DNO's generic BEB, reached by a target mismatch u π ̸ = u n between the distributive profit-squeeze target and the Keynesian normal rate, which moves the equilibrium across Σ at non-zero speed; the resulting crossing limit cycle has amplitude linear in the unfolding (u π-u n) (R 2 ≈ 0.998, against 0.78 for a √ • law), the DNO boundary-focus signature and the empirical discriminator against the smooth Hopf of [1]. The narrative is constructive: the non-smoothness alone cannot cycle (R1-R2); the cycle is born only through the generic unfolding (R3). An independent first-order Melnikov analysis on a conservative Goodwin-Lotka-Volterra core reproduces all three facts by disjoint machinery and adds the count-a single stable cycle near the conservative limit-and a coordinate-free unfolding, the warranted displacement ∆ w = g(x *), unifies the two.

title: Monotone Stability and Structural Containment in Accumulation-Distribution Systems
affiliations: University of Brasília (UnB)

detail.title: Monotone Stability and Structural Containment in Accumulation-Distribution Systems
detail.abstract: We study a nested family of continuous-time accumulation-distribution systems, ordered by how many structural variables-the profit share, the markup, the fiscal stance, the real exchange rate-are made endogenous around a common long-run centre, the Cambridge anchor r * = (g n + δ)/s π. Two results organise the family. First, a monotone stability hierarchy: along the chain the Hopf threshold of the Harrodian accumulation response rises strictly with each endogenised variable, 0 = η (2) H = η (3) H < η (3+) H < η (4) H < η (5) H , with closed-form thresholds in which each level equals its predecessor plus a manifestly positive increment-so a structurally more complete economy tolerates a stronger accumulation response before losing stability. The monotonicity is exact on an explicitly stated range of the layer-specific adjustment speeds; we characterise the boundary of that range, beyond which a layer can cease to stabilise. Second, a containment result: the leading benchmark models-the flexible accelerator, Tobin's q and the New Keynesian Euler equation for investment, the three-equation New Keynesian system, and the Solow-Swan model-arise as restrictions of the family, the last as a measure-zero member; imperfect competition enters through a Cournot-Cambridge condition that pins the number of firms consistent with the anchor. The family is minimal for the structural properties it reproduces. We read the hierarchy not as a verdict on the benchmarks but as the smooth setting that contains them and locates each as a limiting case. Because the Hopf threshold governs only the oscillatory channel, we keep explicit that the real-sector layers are saddles in a separate, real direction-so "below threshold" is not the same as "globally stable".

title: Letter of Credit Disputes from an Arbitration Perspective

detail.title: Letter of Credit Disputes from an Arbitration Perspective
detail.abstract: In a recent study, it might not be possible to refer letter of credit fraud cases to arbitration instead of litigation. Alavi's research suggested that there could be some obstacles, such as obtaining banks' response and cooperation; the different and high standards of proof of fraud required; and the difficulty in obtaining an injunction. His study answered a question proposed by Blodgett and Mayer as to whether arbitration would ever take place in letter of credit disputes. This short research paper will answer this question, but from a different angle: whether arbitration will provide more appropriate judgments (award) than litigation regarding letter of credit disputes. This question arises from the writer's observation that, in the past twenty years, different judgments have been issued for similar disputes.

detail.title: Could Country-by-Country Reporting Increase Profit Shifting?
detail.abstract: Since 2016, Country-by-Country reporting has provided tax authorities with detailed information about multinationals’ worldwide activities. We model Country-by-Country reporting as increasing tax planning and tax audit costs for profit-shifting multinationals, where the latter costs depend on the share of profits in tax havens. Then, Country-by-Country reporting makes shifting profits from a high-tax country to a tax haven more attractive compared to shifting from a low-tax country. Thus, while total profits shifted to the haven decrease, profit shifting from high-tax affiliates may increase relative to the situation without Country-by-Country reporting. We confirm these changes in profit-shifting patterns using a difference-in-differences design.

title: Are Natural Catastrophes and Social Shocks Usable Triggers for Economic Cat Bonds? A Machine Learning Assessment
affiliations: and Universidad Europea de Madrid

detail.title: Are Natural Catastrophes and Social Shocks Usable Triggers for Economic Cat Bonds? A Machine Learning Assessment
detail.abstract: This study evaluates whether environmental and social variables can serve as effective triggers for economic crisis-linked catastrophe bonds using machine learning techniques. We analyze monthly stock market data from four diverse economies-Spain (IBEX 35), the United States (S&P 500), Brazil (Bovespa), and Japan (Nikkei 225)-spanning 1985-2023 (1993-2023 for Spain and Brazil due to index data availability). Employing both XGBoost (gradient boosting) and LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) neural networks with 5-fold time series cross-validation, we assess regression (return prediction) and classification (crisis detection) tasks. Our findings reveal that environmental variables (temperature, precipitation, CO 2 emissions) and social indicators (disaster-affected population) consistently rank among the least important predictors across all countries, with average SHAP importance ranks of 12-17 out of 17 features. Market-derived volatility measures and traditional macroeconomic variables dominate feature importance in both model architectures. While regression models show limited predictive power (XGBoost average R 2 :-0.17; LSTM average R 2 :-0.18), classification models achieve promising results for crisis detection, with AUC values between 0.82 and 0.91. These results suggest that economic CAT bonds would be better served by volatility-based or macroeconomic triggers rather than environmental or social indicators measured at national aggregate levels.

title: Learning from Inaction
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Economics,  and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Economics

detail.title: Learning from Inaction
detail.abstract: We experimentally study how agents extract information from the absence of a signal or action across three canonical settings: an individual state-guessing task, a two-player colored hats game, and an incomplete-information matching market. In each setting, inaction arises naturally from the environment rather than from strategic choice, allowing us to isolate the inferential challenge it poses. We find that learning from inaction is consistently more difficult than learning from action across all three environments. Participants underreact to inaction even when it carries the same informational value as an observed action. We further introduce a treatment that makes inaction explicitly observable. This intervention generally improves learning from inaction, suggesting that a key source of the difficulty is the failure to recognize absence as informative in the first place.

title: Modelling Order Book Imbalance with Hawkes Processes

detail.title: Modelling Order Book Imbalance with Hawkes Processes
detail.abstract: This paper uses Hawkes processes to model cryptocurrency market microstructures. It specifically looks at order flow imbalance. It captures whether the order book, at the next time step, is dominated by buying pressure or by selling pressure. Hawkes processes are stochastic point processes that capture both self-excitations (a big bid arrival causing a surge in bid arrivals) and crossexciting effects such as surge in bid arrivals causing a cascading effect on ask arrivals. We use L2 order book data retrieved via Coinbase web socket API, model the dynamics of order book using Hawkes processes and benchmark it against the existing models such as Avellaneda-Stoikov that utilise Poisson processes.

title: Cross-coin Heterogeneity in Liquidation Cascade Dynamics:Evidence from Meme Coin Perpetual Futures

detail.title: Cross-coin Heterogeneity in Liquidation Cascade Dynamics:Evidence from Meme Coin Perpetual Futures
detail.abstract: Exchange-reported liquidation data is unreliable, with major venues throttling feeds to one event per second. We propose a framework detecting liquidation cascades from public order book data, bypassing exchange-reported feeds. Applying it to three meme coin perpetual futures on OKX-PEPE, BOME, and FLOKI-we document significant cross-coin heterogeneity: positive cascade rates in small-cap coins (BOME 19.4%, FLOKI 18.2%) significantly exceed that of large-cap PEPE (12.5%, p < 0.001). OBI-Bias coupling is positive in BOME (ρ = +0.14, p < 0.001) but negative in PEPE (ρ =-0.23, p < 0.001), suggesting that market structure fundamentally alters the sign of the order book-price relationship. These findings caution against uniform risk parameters across structurally distinct assets.

detail.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence and digital technologies are sharply reducing the cost of acquiring and applying productive knowledge. We develop a labor-market equilibrium model in which knowledge-transfer costs and occupational preferences jointly determine wages. Lower transfer costs increase labor mobility, compress traditional skill premia, and can alter relative wages in unexpected ways. In the limiting case of costless knowledge transfer, occupations traditionally viewed as high skill may earn less than lower-skill occupations if workers strongly prefer them. We also discuss how AIs impact will vary across occupations depending on the extent to which knowledge can be codified, automated, or transferred.

title: The Crossroads of Benthamite Utilitarianism: William Thompsonʼs Critique of James Mill
affiliations: Keio University - Graduate School of Economics

detail.title: The Crossroads of Benthamite Utilitarianism: William Thompsonʼs Critique of James Mill
detail.abstract: This paper aims to clarify a key divergence in Benthamite utilitarian prospects between James Mill and William Thompson̶an issue that has often been discussed within the context of feminism̶by focusing on their contrasting conceptions of the middling class. Mill presents being "freed from manual labor," in addition to the possession of moderate property, as a necessary condition for the middling class. Thompson, by contrast, identifies the relevant condition only as "moderate wealth," distinguished from excessive want and excessive luxury. This conceptual difference enables Thompson to criticize Millʼs distributive argument that, given the conflict between laborers and capitalists, a larger share of wealth should be allocated to the capitalist, and to defend an equal distribution. However, a closer reading also reveals important similarities between them regarding the social functions they assign to the middling class. Although Thompson is often portrayed in hindsight, as a turning point at which utilitarianism moved toward socialism, Thompsonʼs own project was more gradual. He sought to merge Millian plans of social reform with Owenite schemes of "community," and to sketch a concrete program of gradual social reform.

title: Loan Forgiveness, Public Service, and Human Capital Investment
affiliations: University of Virginia, Darden School, University of Chicago and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Loan Forgiveness, Public Service, and Human Capital Investment
detail.abstract: Financial policy is often used to affect labor market outcomes, either through encouraging investment or steering individuals into certain professions. This paper studies how loan forgiveness affects incentives for career choice and performance in the setting of the U.S. medical profession. We exploit the introduction of Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which affects physician labor sorting and hospital performance. We leverage the program's differential value across residency settings where residency years in not-for-profit hospitals count toward forgiveness despite low resident earnings, while training in for-profit hospitals does not. Using a novel and comprehensive dataset compiled from multiple public and private sources on the education and employment choices of physicians in the United States, we find that loan forgiveness increases the probability that physicians training in non-profit hospitals take a non-profit job by about 6 percentage points in our preferred specification. Physicians exhibited sharp uptake in non-profit jobs following the law's introduction. This uptake is sensitive to political discussions around abolishing forgiveness and unconditional loan forgiveness. In states where legal obstacles made forgiveness difficult for physicians, the increase in non-profit job choice is sharply attenuated. We find no evidence that PSLF induces physicians to choose lower-paying specialties; if anything, reform-exposed cohorts training in NFP residencies select into higher-paying specialties, longer training, and fellowships. Non-profit hospitals that benefit from their ability to offer forgiveness exhibit faster growth in physician labor force and revenue, with a lower labor share of expenses following the reform.

detail.abstract: Illegal wildlife trade (IWT) in Eastern Africa constitutes a structural challenge to biodiversity, governance, and regional integration. Although the East African Community (EAC) possesses treaty-based mandates on environmental conservation, natural resource management, and judicial cooperation, wildlife trafficking continues to be addressed predominantly through fragmented domestic frameworks. Meanwhile, the Wildlife Justice Commission (WJC) has developed a model of intelligence-led disruption that recognises wildlife crime as transnational organised crime requiring coordinated enforcement. This article argues that the EAC Treaty contains underdeveloped supranational tools capable of anchoring a regional wildlife justice regime grounded in supremacy, direct effect, harmonisation, and mutual legal assistance (MLA). Through doctrinal analysis of EAC law, comparative regional integration theory, and empirical scholarship on wildlife governance, this article proposes: (1) recognition of wildlife obligations as justiciable under EAC law; (2) adoption of a dedicated EAC Wildlife Crime MLA Protocol; (3) expansion of the environmental jurisdiction of the East African Court of Justice (EACJ); (4) institutionalisation of a Wildlife Sector Coordinating Unit; and (5) formalised strategic partnership frameworks with enforcement actors such as the Wildlife Justice Commission (WJC). By reconceptualising wildlife trafficking as a regional integration issue rather than merely a conservation concern, the EAC can evolve from policy coordination toward enforceable supranational wildlife justice.

detail.abstract: This paper employs the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) as a case study to explore how the concept of the 'Second World', as developed in SWAIL, can serve as an analytical lens for understanding the layered liminality of parts of Eastern Europe, Central Asia and the Caucasus, which experience a strong gravitational pull from two competing integration models: the European Union (EU) and the EAEU. The paper shows that States in these regions experience temporal liminality between a Soviet-imprinted past and divergent future trajectories of full Western integration or Eurasian regionalism. Further, the EU and the EAEU articulate overlapping spatial visions that assign differentiated places to States, reinforcing regional liminality. Finally, the paper argues that the de facto hierarchy within the EAEU that centralises Russian legal authority, perpetuates the liminal condition of the EAEU Member States.

title: Short Dynamic Panels with Cross-Sectional Average Instruments under Multifactor Errors

detail.title: Short Dynamic Panels with Cross-Sectional Average Instruments under Multifactor Errors
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a generalised method of moments estimator for short dynamic panel data models in which the error structure contains unobserved common factors. The estimator combines the cross-sectional average device with internal instrumental variable estimation of the autoregressive parameter. The first-differenced lagged dependent variable is instrumented with lagged levels, which removes the bias that renders least squares estimation of the dynamic coefficient inconsistent under a fixed time dimension, while cross-sectional averages of the levels enter as controls that absorb the factor component. The estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal as the cross-section dimension diverges with the time dimension held fixed, and it does not require the number of factors to be specified. A simulation study shows that the estimator achieves the smallest median bias among competing procedures across a range of factor configurations, including settings in which the number of factors is unknown and in which the factor loadings are correlated with the regressors. The practical value of the estimator is illustrated with two crosscountry growth applications. The first shows that accounting for the factor structure lowers the estimated persistence of output per capita. The second, an income convergence panel, shows that common global shocks explain much of the apparent persistence in crosscountry relative income.

title: Optimal Investment in Annuities and Life Insurance for Retired Couples: The Role of Side Bequest Motives

detail.title: Optimal Investment in Annuities and Life Insurance for Retired Couples: The Role of Side Bequest Motives
detail.abstract: Recent empirical evidence shows that a significant amount of wealth is bequeathed at the death of the first spouse. We study both theoretically and quantitatively how couples' retirement portfolio of annuities and life insurance is affected by such side bequests. We show that life-contingent products allow couples to smooth their side bequests as they enable to make the latter independent of which spouse dies first. We also show that side bequests reduce the wealth left to the surviving spouse while raising the demand for life insurance (or reducing the demand for annuities). Quantitatively, we find that side bequests have a sizable impact on the demand for annuities: annuity participation is 28 percentage points lower for married women and 41 percentage points lower for married men. Finally, we find that side bequests modify the distribution of welfare gains from having access to life-contingent products and that incorrectly omitting side bequest motives in the design of optimal portfolio strategies comes at large welfare costs.

detail.title: Football Empires: Simulating the Effects of Colonialism on the 2026 World Cup

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
European empires extracted vast resources from their colonies and continue to benefit from these legacies today. We examine an under-researched domain of this advantage: international football. Drawing on the literatures on colonial labor extraction, the "muscle drain" in global sports, and cumulative causation, we argue that colonial migration pipelines channel football talent from former colonies to former imperial powers, generating self-reinforcing competitive advantages. We test this argument using approximately 1,500 simulations of the (currently upcoming) FIFA World Cup 2026 tournament in Football Manager under three roster conditions: actual rosters, rosters with colony-background players redistributed to their ex-colonial "heritage nations," and rosters with colony-background players removed entirely. We identify 49 colony-background players across six European teams. 

All four pre-registered hypotheses find support. Former colonizer countries perform significantly worse without colony-background players and formerly colonized countries perform significantly better when they receive them. We also predict the World Cup 2026 results under each condition. France has the highest probability of winning the tournament with actual rosters in our simulations. However, it fields 17 colony-background players and sees its World Cup win rate nearly halve under redistribution of these players, while Brazil's prospects double. Former colonizer teams collectively account for over three-quarters of simulated tournament wins under actual rosters but lose more than 20 percentage points of that share when colony-background talent is redistributed. This study demonstrates that colonial legacies continue to shape competitive outcomes in international football, with consequences for the financial rewards, cultural prestige, and soft power that accompany World Cup success.

title: Climate-driven Financial Risk and Optimal Portfolio Choice with Temperature-linked Derivatives
affiliations: University of Oslo , Sapienza University of Rome - Department of Methods and Models for Economics, Territory and Finance (MEMOTEF) and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Climate-driven Financial Risk and Optimal Portfolio Choice with Temperature-linked Derivatives
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of temperature-related risks on investment decisions and explores how weather derivatives can be incorporated into dynamic portfolio optimization. We model temperature as a stochastic state variable, analogous to longevity in actuarial finance, capturing climate-related uncertainty that cannot be directly traded in financial markets. The model includes two stochastic factors, namely the interest rate and temperature, described by Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and Vasicek-type processes, respectively. To manage both financial and temperature risk, we consider a portfolio comprising a risky asset, a rolling zero-coupon bond, a money market account, and temperature-linked derivatives. By solving the corresponding stochastic control problem under constant relative risk aversion (CRRA) preferences, we obtain closed-form expressions for the optimal portfolio weights and value function. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that including temperature derivatives provides significant economic benefits. Optimal allocations to the derivatives dynamically adjust to seasonal temperature patterns, efficiently hedging exogenous climate risk and influencing the allocation to other assets. We quantify these gains through portfolio improvement measures, Willingness-to-Pay, and downside risk reduction, showing that the derivatives enhance both expected wealth and the probability of achieving long-term investment targets. These results highlight that temperature-linked derivatives can make non-financial risks financially manageable, extending classical portfolio theory to incorporate climate risk.

title: Sense of Responsibility for Ecological Restoration
affiliations: National Research Council of Italy, University of Bologna, Department of Economics, Institute of Cognitive Sciences and Technologies, University of Bologna - Department of Economics and National Research Council (CNR)

detail.title: Sense of Responsibility for Ecological Restoration
detail.abstract: Climate change and biodiversity loss require not only conservation, but also collective efforts to restore degraded ecosystems. Yet restoration often depends on costly individual contributions to a public good, making it vulnerable to free-riding and misperceptions about others' willingness to act. We study these challenges in a lab experiment (N=812) consisting of two stages: extraction from a shared virtual forest followed by restoration. We examine whether individuals' prior exploitation affects restoration, whether restoration differs when damage is repaired by those that caused it or by others, and whether correcting misperceptions about others' sense of responsibility influences restoration. We find no evidence that individuals who extract more are less willing to restore, nor that restoration is significantly higher when performed by a group different from the one that caused the damage. In contrast, responsibility beliefs play a central role. Individuals who feel more responsible contribute more to restoration, yet they systematically underestimate others' sense of responsibility, generating widespread pluralistic ignorance. Correcting this misperception through information provision does not increase restoration on average. Instead, it produces heterogeneous responses: relatively cooperative individuals increase restoration, whereas more opportunistic individuals reduce it, consistent with strategic free-riding. Overall, our findings identify sense of responsibility and misperceptions of others' responsibility as key determinants of ecological restoration, suggesting that information-based interventions may backfire and informing policies for ecosystem recovery after environmental degradation.

detail.abstract: Financial inclusion in Africa presents a puzzle: while digital and physical access has expanded dramatically, the usage of financial services has not improved in many countries. The purpose of this study is to compare the performance of 46 African countries towards financial inclusion; to achieve this, a composite Financial Inclusion Index (FII) has been created across four Global Findex waves (2011, 2014, 2017 and 2021). Apart from comparing these countries' performance on financial inclusion, this study also used decomposition analysis to examine whether a country's financial services lack access, quality, usage, or other dimensions. The literature review section also highlights that this study is a unique piece of work, as no existing study has focused on decomposing the gap in the financial inclusion index using access, usage, and quality as indicators on the African continent. The study identified three distinct growth trajectories as Leaders, Stalled, and Breakout Performers and shows how internal dimension conflicts explain stagnation in nations. The study will help policymakers decide whether their priority should be expanding infrastructure, activating usage through digital payments, or strengthening governance in the context of a particular country on the African continent.

detail.title: Segment Information Disclosure and Trade Credit
detail.abstract: We examine the effect of mandatory segment disclosure on trade credit financing. Segment disclosure reduces the information advantage of suppliers relative to investors in evaluating firm default risk, reducing firms' reliance on trade credit. Exploiting the adoption of SFAS 131 as a shock to segment disclosure, we find that segment disclosure reduces reliance on trade credit among disclosing firms. This effect is stronger for firms with high ex-ante default risk, poor information environments, and weak governance. Further analysis shows that segment disclosure reduces perceived default risk, eases financial constraints, increases stock liquidity, and facilitates the issuance of informationally sensitive securities.

title: Who Elected Anthropic?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Who Elected Anthropic?
detail.abstract: This essay argues that Anthropic did not capture the AI regulatory environment, it constituted it. Through the Responsible Scaling Policy, now on version 3.3, Anthropic established the capability thresholds, risk classifications, evaluation methodology, and governance vocabulary that the UK AI Safety Institute, EU frontier-model policy, and U.S. voluntary safety commitments subsequently adopted. The essay traces how a private safety framework becomes public governance architecture: not through mandate but through availability, as the institution that produces the conceptual architecture before regulators arrive defines what governance means. The essay argues that the RSP functions not as a constraint on Anthropic but as a credential, a standard the firm wrote for itself, assesses itself, and revises itself. It examines how Anthropic's principled Pentagon refusal, Vatican encyclical co-presentation, and revenue trajectory are structurally identical outcomes of the same governance strategy. The essay concludes that Anthropic's approaching IPO is the moment the mission and capital grammars must appear in the same document, revealing that the near-trillion-dollar valuation is pricing institutional authority over the definition of safety itself. Part of the Synthetic Civilization political economy series.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the moral purpose of law through the relationship between justice, mercy, accountability, human dignity, and the spirit of law. It asks whether law is primarily a tool of punishment, correction, guidance, protection, deterrence, institutional restraint, or revenge. Written from the perspective of an interdisciplinary researcher rather than a practising lawyer, the paper argues that legal systems derive legitimacy not only from formal rules, but also from the moral intelligence with which those rules are interpreted, applied, and restrained. It begins with an Islamic ethical reflection on divine mercy, repentance, and accountability, then moves through ancient legal codes, constitutional restraint, due process, fair-trial guarantees, procedural safeguards, judicial discretion, restorative justice, executive clemency, and unequal access to legal representation. The central argument is that the letter of the law and the spirit of the law should not be treated as enemies. The spirit of law does not abolish the text; it asks the text to remember its purpose: to protect society, restrain power, repair harm, distinguish deliberate evil from human weakness, and prevent justice from becoming revenge.

title:
Twenty-Five Years of Competition Policy and Market Concentration in Armenia
Evidence Before and After the 2018 Velvet Revolution
affiliations: California Polytechnic State University

detail.title:
Twenty-Five Years of Competition Policy and Market Concentration in Armenia
Evidence Before and After the 2018 Velvet Revolution
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates whether Armenia's 2018 Velvet Revolution changed the country's competitive environment. Using annual reports of Armenia's competition authority and a market-level panel compiled from those reports, the paper separates two outcomes that are often conflated in public debate: the activity of the competition authority and the structure of the markets it regulates. The distinction matters. The evidence assembled here suggests a clear change in enforcement intensity after 2018, including more proceedings, broader sectoral studies, larger penalties, and more visible merger review. The evidence on market structure is more cautious. Available CR3 observations across major product markets do not show a broad decline in concentration after the revolution. If anything, the average reported CR3 is essentially unchanged between the pre-revolution and post-revolution periods. The strongest conclusion is therefore not that the revolution failed, and not that it fully dismantled oligarchic market power. The defensible conclusion is narrower and more important: the revolution appears to have changed the enforcement state faster than it changed the market structure.

title: Does Easier Alcohol Access Affect Road Safety? Insights from Texas Municipal Elections
affiliations: and Purdue University

detail.title: Does Easier Alcohol Access Affect Road Safety? Insights from Texas Municipal Elections
detail.abstract: We examine whether legalizing local alcohol sales affects traffic safety, exploiting close local option elections in Texas as a quasi-random source of variation. Over 300 Texas cities voted to legalize alcohol sales between 2003 and 2019. Legalization generated large increases in off-premise alcohol licenses (liquor stores and grocery stores) with little change in on-premise establishments, and shifted alcohol sales from bars and restaurants toward retail outlets for home consumption. Despite these large changes in access, we find no meaningful increase in total crashes, DUI crashes, or fatal crashes, and no evidence of spillover effects on neighboring cities. This null result reflects which type of access was expanded: on-premise licenses are positively associated with crash rates while off-premise licenses are not, consistent with bars and restaurants (not retail stores) being the channel through which alcohol access raises traffic risk.

title: Significance Without Substance: How Overlapping Observations Inflate an Insider-Trading Signal

detail.title: Significance Without Substance: How Overlapping Observations Inflate an Insider-Trading Signal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author developed the quantitative trading system from which the data pipeline and signal definitions used in this study originate. The author has no financial relationship with any third party that could be perceived to have influenced this study. The analysis evaluates the author's own signal and reports a null result.

detail.abstract: Cluster buying by corporate insiders-multiple insiders purchasing the same stock within a short window-is widely regarded as a strong predictor of future returns. Using point-in-time S&P 500 membership and EDGAR Form-4 filings from 2015 to 2024, we document a 12-week forward return spread between cluster-buy and noactivity stocks that is significant at 𝑝 ≈ 1.6 × 10-9 under a conventional two-sample test. This significance does not survive correction for the overlapping, cross-correlated structure of the underlying observations. Under Newey-West HAC standard errors, a stationary block-bootstrap, and non-overlapping subsampling, the 𝑝-value rises to approximately 0.6-0.7, and the mean weekly spread is statistically indistinguishable from zero (-0.17%, 95% CI [-1.19%, +0.85%]). We isolate two inflation channels and show that the dominant one is not autocorrelation per se but the pooling of overlapping within-week observations as if independent; the entire visible effect concentrates in the 2020 regime. The signal that appears overwhelmingly significant under naive testing is, under correct inference, not distinguishable from noise.

title: A Theory for Why Large Farms need Small Farms
affiliations: and INRA

detail.title: A Theory for Why Large Farms need Small Farms
detail.abstract: The political economy literature related to agricultural policy provides a number of conjectures corresponding to farm size, but provides no theoretical model of the political utility of small farms. Framed in the context of regulation, we demonstrate how large farms may use small farms to influence their regulatory burden. Producing in the presence of externalities, farms can be regulated to eliminate the damage. We compare a socially optimal regulation with the choice that would be taken by a large farm if it could influence the regulatory decision using the small farm as political cover. Compared to the socially optimal choice, there are cases where the large farm would choose regulation and reduced competition while in others would choose to fight the regulation to save its smaller rival. If the externality and the regulatory burden are very large, the large farm prefers more competition if that leads to less regulation. In this case, lobbying to "save small farms" is in the best interest of the large farm.

title:
The Automatable and the Engaged 
How AI Makes the Case for Action Research in Management Scholarship

detail.title:
The Automatable and the Engaged 
How AI Makes the Case for Action Research in Management Scholarship
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence forces an old question into a harder form: what is intrinsically human, what can only a human do? This essay pursues the question within management scholarship. The field has long argued about its worth through two oppositions-rigor against relevance, and the quantitative against the qualitative-and I argue that artificial intelligence is dissolving both. The line that now matters runs elsewhere, and it cuts through every method rather than between them: between the automatable component of inquiry, which AI is rapidly making abundant and cheap, and the engaged component, which depends on being in the world, acting in it, and being answerable for the action. Action research, defined by that engagement rather than by any technique, is the clearest case of inquiry a machine cannot perform. The argument has consequences for how the field trains, judges, and rewards its scholars-and for a prestige system that, just now, is rewarding the automatable and withdrawing from the engaged.

title:
Ecological Niches and Strategy Choice 
How Constraint Regimes Compress and Expand Social Differences

detail.title:
Ecological Niches and Strategy Choice 
How Constraint Regimes Compress and Expand Social Differences

detail.abstract: This paper develops a niche-based framework for explaining why social differences are compressed in some environments and amplified in others. The core claim is that inequality is not only a distribution of resources; it is also a context-specific conversion process through which marginal resources become separations in safety, autonomy, time control, and life quality. I define this conversion process as elasticity: a family of dimensionspecific slopes by which resources and buffers translate into outcome separation under a given constraint regime. In low-elasticity environments, such as trenches, confined transport systems, or frontline emergency settings, shared constraints and synchronized exposure cap the practical value of additional resources. In highelasticity environments, such as housing, asset accumulation, education pipelines, and institutional navigation, resources can purchase separation, insulation, and compounding advantage. The paper links ecological niche, constraint regime, elasticity, and strategy set: different environments do not merely distribute unequal outcomes; they also make different strategies rational. Low-elasticity settings tend to reward discipline, cooperation, and gap-restraint, while high-elasticity settings reward gatekeeping, signaling, and intergenerational closure. The framework predicts that the same marginal resource will have weaker effects on immediate exposure under synchronized shock, but stronger and more compounding effects under slow attrition when it can buy time, exit, or institutional priority.

title: Bridging the Scalability Gap in Digital Servitization: Asset Decoupling, Operational Integration, and the Limits of Service-Led Growth

detail.title: Bridging the Scalability Gap in Digital Servitization: Asset Decoupling, Operational Integration, and the Limits of Service-Led Growth
detail.abstract: Industrial firms that pursue service-led growth rarely scale the way digital-native firms do. This paper argues that the difference turns on two firm-level conditions rather than on "digitalization" in general. The first is capital posture-the degree to which a firm is decoupled from owning and financing the physical assets behind the service. The second is operational integration-the degree to which a firm's digital systems are embedded in the downstream workflows that complete service actions, whether the firm enables that completion (as an infrastructure provider) or executes it directly. Crossing the two conditions yields a typology with a single high-scalability region (asset-light and highly integrated) and two characteristic failure modes: the alert-fatigue trap, where information is generated but action is left to the customer, and the balance-sheet drag, where service growth consumes provider capital. We specify the constructs, decompose each into measurable components, derive a mechanistic set of propositions distinguishing customer-side coordination costs from provider-side capital intensity, and reinterpret the digitalservitization-versus-service-digitalization debate as a question of which condition a firm secures first. We add a demand-side moderator-customer adoption readiness-under which a technically scalable firm can remain commercially blocked. The framework contributes to the special issue by explaining scalability as the joint outcome of asset decoupling and operational integration in digital servitization, and it is illustrated with named business-to-business ventures used strictly as conceptual exemplars.

title: Averting Long and Casualised hours in the Future of Work: Working Time in the ILO's Second Discussion on Decent Work in the Platform Economy
affiliations: Durham University - Law School

detail.title: Averting Long and Casualised hours in the Future of Work: Working Time in the ILO's Second Discussion on Decent Work in the Platform Economy
detail.abstract: In June 2026, the ILO International Labour Conference is aiming to agree upon international standards – a Convention and Recommendation - on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. The Conference will reflect on crucial, facets of platform work that include how to define, count, and remunerate working hours. The working time elements of this standard-setting process are significant: international standards on platform work would be influential on the conceptualisation and regulation of working time in countries across the world (in working relationships organised through digital labour platforms and in a range of other jobs). This Policy Briefing examines the working time dimension of the Conference’s ‘second discussion’ on platform work. It suggests how the draft standards’ protective clauses (hours limits, rest periods) could be strengthened and highlights the risk to fully-waged working hours that is posed by the treatment of “waiting time.”

title: Governance as a Product (GaaP): A Reputation-Weighted Institutional Architecture for Autonomous AI Agent Governance
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title: Governance as a Product (GaaP): A Reputation-Weighted Institutional Architecture for Autonomous AI Agent Governance
detail.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents already act consequentially in finance, medicine, and critical infrastructure, yet the governance that binds them remains either informal and unenforceable or formal and institutionally inoperable. This paper argues that human legal governance fails for two interacting reasons: natural language cannot fully describe the situations governance must cover, and human institutions reason about the rules they do state unreliably. We present Governance as a Product (GaaP), a callable and composable governance service that addresses both failures through a reputation-weighted institutional architecture rather than a restricted formal logic. GaaP composes four interdependent layers: a weighted directed acyclic graph substrate with non-transferable reputation staking; a translation and validation layer that pairs typed governance primitives and ontology-guided composition with reputationstaked validation pools; deterministic cryptoeconomic enforcement; and a temporal layer in which the system governs its own evolution. The architecture trades a formal completeness guarantee for full expressiveness and institutional operability, reducing reasoning error to a bounded and auditable residual. We position GaaP as durable and adaptive infrastructure for the sustainable governance of autonomous systems, able to evolve without ossifying and so to remain valid as technology and norms shift.

The citation channel dominates: ecosystem coordination elevated measured impact metrics, attracting additional submissions and generating article-processingcharge revenue through publication volume. The findings speak to the economics of coordinated networks in information-goods markets.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the long-term impact of working capital management (WCM) on share price performance in Pakistan's textile sector. Using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analysis on a panel dataset of 10 textile companies listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) from 2016 to 2025, we find that the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) has a significant negative relationship with share prices (coefficient:-5.8, p < 0.01), indicating that shorter cash recovery cycles enhance market valuation. Inventory turnover shows a strong positive association with share prices (coefficient: 8.43, p < 0.01), while receivable days exhibit a significant negative effect (coefficient:-4.85, p < 0.05). The current ratio and payable days show no statistically significant relationship with share prices. High-efficiency firms (average CCC: 44 days) outperform low-efficiency firms (average CCC: 71 days) by a substantial margin of Rs. 299.6 in average share price. These findings contribute to the literature by demonstrating the dominant role of CCC in driving shareholder value in an emerging market context, shifting focus from traditional profitability metrics to market-based valuation outcomes.

title: FedCoda: Calibrating and Debiasing Prototypes for Federated Domain Generalization
affiliations: Beijing Institute of Technology, City University of Macau, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Institute of Software, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology, Technical University of Denmark and Beijing Institute of Technology

detail.title: FedCoda: Calibrating and Debiasing Prototypes for Federated Domain Generalization
detail.abstract: Federated domain generalization aims to learn a global model that generalizes well to unseen domains. Feature alignment with prototypes enhances domain-invariant representation learning, aligning inconsistent feature spaces caused by domain skew. However, we identify two key problems that limits feature alignment: local prototypes become unreliable due to mismatched batch normalization statistics and insufficient inter-class separation, while conventional prototype aggregation biases the global feature space toward overrepresented domains. Building on these findings, we propose FedCoda, a cross-domain feature alignment framework that calibrates local prototype geometry and debiases global prototype aggregation. FedCoda first performs calibrated feature alignment by transitioning to global batch normalization statistics in the later training stage, while introducing a prototype calibration loss that encourages well-separated class prototypes. It then applies fair prototype aggregation, which optimizes global prototypes by minimizing the variance of their distances to local prototypes, reducing dominance from domains with more clients. Extensive experiments show that FedCoda consistently improves generalization ability and representation learning under various settings, demonstrating the importance of jointly addressing prototype reliability and aggregation fairness for federated domain generalization.

title: Charged Up: Impacts of Green Energy Transition on Local Labor Markets
affiliations: University of Manchester - Department of Economics and Clemson University, John E. Walker Department of Economics

detail.title: Charged Up: Impacts of Green Energy Transition on Local Labor Markets
detail.abstract: This paper studies the effects of utility-scale renewable energy expansion on local labor markets in the United States from 2005 to 2019. Utilizing exogenous solar and wind potentials from remote sensing data, we find a positive employment effect from solar and wind energy, and the effects are not short-lived. Solar energy also contributes to small wage growth. We find notable increases in jobs and business establishments in many sectors, particularly manufacturing in support of a local agglomeration effect. These gains are very localized, reflected in strong in-migration and weak local spillover. The gains are mostly concentrated among younger and lower-educated workers.

title: Hidden Damages: Facing Heterogeneity in the Effects of Air Pollution on Regional GDP
affiliations: RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment, RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment and RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment

detail.title: Hidden Damages: Facing Heterogeneity in the Effects of Air Pollution on Regional GDP
detail.abstract: Standard estimates of the economic costs of air pollution assume (directly or indirectly) that causal effects and instrument strength are homogeneous across regions. We relax this assumption and show that it matters. Using a panel of European NUTS3 regions from 2000 to 2022, we estimate the effect of $PM_{2.5}$ on regional GDP per capita through a strategy that jointly accounts for heterogeneity in both the instruments' first stage and the causal response. For the average effect, we implement the Flexible IV (FIV) estimator from the Double-Debiased Machine Learning literature, allowing instrument strength to vary across biogeographical regions. Our preferred estimate is a 0.3 percent decline in GDP per capita per $\mu g/m^3$ increase in annual $PM_{2.5}$ --- approximately one-third of the reported by conventional two-stage least squares specifications in previous work. Coupling the FIV with an IV Causal Forest yields conditional causal responses that span $-1.22$ to $0.1$ percent, with a long left tail. Statistically significant heterogeneity is driven by regional dependence on agriculture and manufacturing, and by historical exposure to pollution, reflecting the interplay between vulnerability and adaptive capacity. We then allocate the localized damage estimates across income quintiles using microdata from the EU Labor Force Survey and the Survey on Income and Living Conditions. The resulting distributional pattern is non-monotonic: middle-income quintiles bear the largest proportional losses while the top quintile is the least affected.

title: Green Transition: Who Pays the Bill? Distributional Effects of Climate Policies
affiliations: University of Trieste

detail.title: Green Transition: Who Pays the Bill? Distributional Effects of Climate Policies
detail.abstract: This paper studies the relationship between green transition policies and inequality in a two-agent overlapping generations (OLG) model, where individuals derive utility also from environmental quality.  The framework features heterogeneous agents in terms of human capital endowments, access to financial markets, and adaptation capacity. Government stabilizes public spending and the debt-to-capital ratio while levying carbon taxes as well as income ones. The Central Bank pegs money growth at a constant rate.At equilibrium, in the absence of targeted policies, the burden of the green transition falls disproportionately on low-skilled agents and increases pre-existing disparities. The analysis identifies the appropriate policy mix allowing restoring equality and/or infra- as well intra-generational efficiency. More in details, to counter the regressive impact of the carbon tax a redistributive policy aiming at subsidizing adaptation is required.

title: Driving Change: The Impact of Low Emission Zones on Commuting Behaviors
affiliations: UCLouvain - UCLouvain Saint-Louis,  and University of Liège

detail.title: Driving Change: The Impact of Low Emission Zones on Commuting Behaviors

keywords.keywords: Low emission zone · Modal shift · Commuting behavior

detail.abstract: Low Emission Zones (LEZs) have emerged as a widely adopted policy instrument aimed at reducing urban air pollution by restricting access for the most polluting vehicles. While substantial research has examined their environmental effectiveness, comparatively little attention has been devoted to their impact on mobility behavior. Using a difference-in-differences strategy applied to Belgian commuter data, this paper estimates the causal effect of the Brussels LEZ on modal choice. By defining the treatment at the level of the commute itself, we are able to examine whether modal reallocation differs by residential and workplace exposure. The results show that individuals living within the LEZ and commuting to workplaces outside the zone reduce car use by 5.8 pp and increase train use by 4.8 pp. These effects vary across income groups, public transport accessibility, and commuting distance.

title: EXTINCTION RISK AND CONSERVATION UNDER CONTINUOUS MANAGEMENT
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice - Dipartimento di Economia

detail.title: EXTINCTION RISK AND CONSERVATION UNDER CONTINUOUS MANAGEMENT
detail.abstract: This paper studies optimal conservation policy under extinction risk in a stochastic framework where population dynamics are subject to environmental uncertainty and extinction is modeled as an absorbing boundary. Building on the real options approach, we extend the existing extinction-risk switching framework by allowing intervention to operate through continuous, state-dependent management rather than through a discrete change in biological parameters. In our framework, a planner can irreversibly switch to a regime that enables continuous control of the population drift at a convex cost, introducing a joint decision over the timing and intensity of intervention. The problem is characterized by coupled variational inequalities and solved numerically.The results show that continuous management introduces an additional margin of adjustment in conservation policy design: instead of a simple threshold rule, intervention is concentrated over intermediate population states, where the trade-off between extinction risk and management costs is most pronounced, and conservation policy involves adjusting both when and how intensively to intervene. Higher environmental volatility expands the intervention region toward relatively fragile ecological states. This reflects the interaction between precautionary extinction-risk considerations and the classical real-options value of waiting.

title: Industrial emission dynamics, eco-efficiency and rebound effects
affiliations: , Lewis & Clark College - Department of Economics and Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU)

detail.title: Industrial emission dynamics, eco-efficiency and rebound effects
detail.abstract: This paper measures emission rebound effects by estimating the elasticity of emissions with respect to eco-efficiency in Swedish manufacturing (2002–2020). We first derive a parsimonious microeconomic framework identifying three structural determinants of rebound: emission cost share, demand elasticity, and abatement efforts. Eco-efficiency for CO2, SO2, and NOx is computed under a by-production framework, and a dynamic panel model (system GMM) links emissions to efficiency, abatement expenditure, demand conditions, and EU ETS exposure. We find pervasive short-run rebound effects, with backfire arising in several sectors. Long-run rebound is weaker and pollutant-specific. CO2 rebound declines modestly across ETS phases, whereas SO2 and NOx display limited phase variation. Efficiency heterogeneity across firms does not generate systematic differences in rebound intensity. Overall, rebound effects reflect structural production responses consistent with the theoretical determinants identified in the model.

title: International Emissions Trading with Asymmetric Transboundary Externalities
affiliations: National Taipei University, Tunghai University and National Chengchi University (NCCU)

detail.title: International Emissions Trading with Asymmetric Transboundary Externalities
detail.abstract: This study examines the efficiency and welfare implications of International Emissions Trading (IET) in the presence of asymmetric transboundary externalities. We build up a model where countries internalize both perfectly transboundary greenhouse gases (e.g., CO₂) and localized co-pollutants (e.g., PM2.5). Our results show that heightened local environmental concerns trigger strategic over-issuance of permits, leading to higher global emissions under IET compared to autarky. Moreover, the transition to IET results in a welfare loss for the permit buyer, while the effect on the seller is indeterminate. The numerical simulation indicates that IET can be detrimental to global welfare even under moderate localized externalities. These findings suggest that the exclusive focus on perfectly transboundary pollution in the previous literature may lead to overly optimistic assessments of the IET regime.

title: Search Ripples in Housing Markets: Quality, Location, and the Housing Cycle
