detail.abstract: This article investigates housing-market search intensity as a measure of within-city market tightness. We use novel transaction-level auction data that distinguish two stages of observed search participation, registered interest and bidding. In line with a stylized model of segmented housing search, we find that search intensity varies systematically across quality tiers. During boom periods, search intensity is relatively higher for lower-quality dwellings. During bust periods, this gradient weakens and partly reverses toward higherquality dwellings. Asking prices are more strongly negatively associated with bidding than with registered interest, consistent with bidding representing a later stage of participation. Quality-specific search intensity is also associated with price growth in the expected direction, and dynamic analyses suggest that changes in search intensity tend to precede changes in prices. These findings point to search intensity as an early indicator of market tightness and as a margin through which housing cycles may propagate across quality and location segments.

title: The Readability of Reality: Information, Consciousness, and the Metaphysics of Meaning
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Readability of Reality: Information, Consciousness, and the Metaphysics of Meaning
detail.abstract:
This monograph advances a cumulative philosophical argument for what it terms the ‘readability thesis’: the claim that the universe exhibits persistent structural compatibility with intelligibility, symbolic information, consciousness, moral awareness, and existential orientation in a manner that exceeds what a purely mechanistic account of nature can coherently explain. The argument does not proceed from alleged gaps in scientific explanation—a strategy that remains permanently vulnerable to the progress of inquiry—but rather from the philosophically significant convergence of phenomena that collectively suggest a deeper ontological orientation within the fabric of existence itself. 
Drawing on resources from philosophy of science, philosophy of mind, metaphysics, and Qurʾānic epistemology, the work develops its thesis across three interconnected investigations. Part One examines the intelligibility of the cosmos: the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics, the informational architecture of biological systems, and the extraordinary precision of cosmological fine- tuning. Part Two turns to the interior dimensions of existence: the irreducibility of subjective consciousness, the epistemological problem posed by the human orientation toward truth, the phenomenology of moral obligation and aesthetic experience, and the universal human confrontation with mortality and transcendence. Part Three situates these inquiries within the framework of Qurʾānic epistemology, arguing that the classical Islamic concept of āyāt—reality as a field of intelligible signs—provides a philosophically sophisticated account of how nature, consciousness, and revelation may be understood as interconnected dimensions of communicative intelligibility. The study concludes by arguing for tawḥīd—divine unity—not merely as theological assertion but as the most coherent metaphysical explanation for why reality consistently and cumulatively discloses rather than conceals. 
The work engages throughout with thinkers including Eugene Wigner, Thomas Nagel, David Chalmers, Alvin Plantinga, Roger Penrose, Paul Davies, Viktor Frankl, Charles Taylor, David Bentley Hart, Toshihiko Izutsu, Muḥammad Iqbal, Seyyed Hossein Nasr, and Fazlur Rahman, among others.

title: AfCFTA, Strategic Gateways and the Geography of African Export Direction

detail.title: AfCFTA, Strategic Gateways and the Geography of African Export Direction
detail.abstract: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is intended to deepen intra-African exchange, but the commercial use of a continental market also depends on transport corridors, maritime gateways and the composition of national exports. This paper examines export direction in a purposively selected sample of eleven African gateway economies over 2017 to 2024, linking country-level CEPII BACI HS17 bilateral product flows to source documented gateway contexts without claiming that exports moved through the named gateways or were caused by port governance. A restricted seven-economy subset is retained as a nested benchmark for testing sample composition sensitivity. Across the eleven economies the weighted intra-African export share is 18.01 per cent, below the 21.71 per cent benchmark; and, unlike the benchmark, excluding South Africa no longer raises that share, which instead falls to 16.34 per cent. The four selected West African economies record 20.98 per cent against 9.84 per cent for the two North African additions, and Africa orientation falls sharply for machinery and chemical products. These shifts reflect the regional and product composition of the selected sample, not an estimated gateway effect. The paper concludes that pooled trade-orientation measures obscure regional, product and destination heterogeneity, and that AfCFTA implementation research should report these dimensions alongside any headline intra-African share.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Law and Empirical Analysis 2026, Vol. 3(1) 105–126

detail.abstract: With the rise of standard contracts, tensions persist between protecting consumers from unfair terms and preserving freedom of contract. A key concern is that consumers may waive legal rights, often unknowingly, particularly when dealing with trusted brands. To address this, we conducted a conjoint experiment with a representative US sample to evaluate how consumers value legal rights-such as warranties, liability, privacy, and conflict resolution-when they are fully aware, understand the terms, and must trade them off against product features like price and brand reputation. Our findings reveal that even when rights can be traded off against other features of the product, consumers value legal rights. Of the legal rights we tested, warranties and price were found to be the most decisive factors in their purchase decisions. Notably, we did not find evidence that brand reputation significantly alters the valuation of legal rights. These insights offer important empirical evidence to enrich the extensive policy debate.

detail.abstract: Over the past fifty years, Massachusetts systematically dismantled most of its large custodial institutions — state schools for people with developmental disabilities, chronic state hospitals, tuberculosis sanitoria, county poor farms — on the principle that people deserve care in settings designed around treatment and dignity rather than custody and segregation. One institution survived every wave of reform: Bridgewater State Hospital, a psychiatric facility operated by the Department of Correction, housing civilly committed individuals in a medium-security prison under correctional protocols, in a structure whose governing authority traces to a legislative act of 1919. This article argues that the Bridgewater debate is not primarily a hospital administration question. It is the unfinished chapter of a civil-rights project Massachusetts has led nationally. Drawing on more than a decade of Disability Law Center monitoring reports, the legal frameworks established by Olmstead v. L.C. and the Marsters v. Healey settlement, and the author's direct experience in the Rolland consent decree implementation, the article examines why Bridgewater survived, what completing the deinstitutionalization journey would require, and why the aging and disability policy community has both the standing and the obligation to insist that it does.

title: The Medium Layer and the Self-Choking AI Economy: Competitive Capacity Crowding, Demand-Realization Collapse, and Phantom Demand

detail.title: The Medium Layer and the Self-Choking AI Economy: Competitive Capacity Crowding, Demand-Realization Collapse, and Phantom Demand
detail.abstract:
The current expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure exhibits a puzzling macropattern that resists conventional explanation: training-side capacity is chronically undersupplied and capital-saturated, while consumer-side AI adoption remains persistently sluggish and underpenetrated, simultaneously. We argue that this configuration is neither a speculative bubble nor a conventional supply constraint, but the signature of a previously unrecognized, endogenous self-inhibiting growth mechanism rooted in the industry's physical resource structure. 
We develop a conceptual and analytical architecture organized around several novel primitives. First, unlike prior digital economies, the AI economy possesses a Hardware Medium Layer-a physically necessary conduit (AI PCs, AI smartphones, on-device accelerators, edge devices) through which AI capability must pass to reach end users and be monetized. We establish four "rigidities" (latency, privacy, cost, and physical possession) that render this layer non-bypassable. Second, we introduce demand realization and realized market formation to distinguish latent willingness-to-pay from the portion that is actually converted into industry revenue through the medium layer; this conversion is bounded not only by budgets and preferences but by the medium's physical throughput. Third, we identify and formalize Competitive Capacity Crowding (CCC): because the training side and the consumer medium draw on the same scarce upstream manufacturing resources-advanced-node wafers, highbandwidth memory (HBM), advanced packaging-their expansions are rivalrous rather than complementary, inverting the standard complementarity logic of general-purpose-technology theory. Fourth, we show that CCC propagates through two channels-demand-side revenue erosion and cost-side budget crowding-reaching every class of institutional buyer without exception (a universal-incidence result). Fifth, we define phantom demand as genuine latent demand rendered unmonetizable by medium compression, and self-inhibiting growth as the resulting dynamic in which industry expansion erodes its own demand base. 
We construct a rigorous three-layer mathematical model-resource allocation, medium formation, and strategic training-side payoffs-and prove a sequence of results: (i) trainingside and medium-side allocations are one-for-one rival under the binding resource constraint; (ii) realized market formation is decreasing, and beyond a critical threshold collapsing nonlinearly, in training-side allocation; (iii) phantom demand accumulates monotonically as the training side expands; (iv) decentralized strategic incentives in an arms-race environment generate socially excessive training-side allocation; and (v) because the binding constraint is physical rather than financial, conventional monetary policy is largely ineffective at restoration. We then provide a complete empirical research design (shift-share instruments, threshold regression, structural VAR, event studies), a thorough discussion of boundary conditions and counterarguments, and policy implications centered on restoring mediumlayer throughput rather than subsidizing compute alone. The broader lesson transcends AI: in resource-intensive technological revolutions, aggressive infrastructure investment can endogenously choke the very demand it seeks to serve.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how heterogeneous trading behavior of retail investors, identified through account-level data and a stockholding-based clustering approach, translates into market impact. Prevalent "retail-as-noise" view masks crucial systematic differences that distinctly shape market quality. Specifically, Premium Speculators, who prefer high-price-and-attention and shell-value stocks, are associated with lower future returns, consistent with overreaction to short-term price movements and underreaction to fundamentals. detail.abstract: This study investigates the institutional determinants of financial inclusion for 15 developing countries in the period after the global financial crisis from 2010 to 2023 using panel fixed effect estimation. The results show that institutional quality has a significant impact on financial inclusion in developing countries. Specifically, higher regulatory quality increases the level of financial inclusion through greater ATM penetration and bank branch expansion, but it decreases bank account ownership. Higher voice and accountability increase financial inclusion through higher ATM penetration. Greater political stability increases financial inclusion through higher bank account ownership and bank branch expansion. Corruption control increases financial inclusion through higher bank account ownership. The interaction analyses show that high regulatory quality during periods of economic prosperity improves financial inclusion through higher bank account ownership. Also, high voice and accountability during periods of economic prosperity leads to greater bank branch expansion which improves financial inclusion. The results of this study demonstrate that, to increase the level of financial inclusion, government should ensure a sound and strong institutional and macroeconomic environment along with strengthening banks and urging them to extend banking services to those who need it.

title: The (Square)-Root of the 2/3 Labor Share

detail.title: The (Square)-Root of the 2/3 Labor Share
detail.abstract: This paper views the aggregate production function as an emerging property of the dynamic evolution of individual firms' labor-and capital productivities. The shape of the aggregate production at any given time is governed by the distribution of underlying firm productivities. I give the class of firm productivities that result in a Cobb-Douglas aggregate production function and present a dynamic model in which this class of firm productivies arises endogenoulsy as the consequence of idiosyncratic shocks to underlying firm productivity. The model generates tractable predictions for firm size and capital intensity. On the balanced growth path the labor share is generally higher than 1/2 and for a broad set of parameters it equals 64%. In particular, a uniform increase in automation intensity does not change the labor share.

detail.abstract: Digital payment infrastructures are increasingly central to how small and medium-sized enterprises seek liquidity, conduct trade, and establish financial credibility. Yet the benefits of digitalization remain uneven, especially in cross-border contexts where payment systems, data regimes, regulatory standards, and financing models remain fragmented. This article develops a four-layer conceptual framework linking payment infrastructure, data and access regimes, financing intermediation, and SME outcomes. Using Nigeria and Poland as illustrative comparative cases, the article examines how mobile-first, platform-centric ecosystems in emerging markets differ from bank-integrated, regulation-driven systems in developed European economies. The analysis shows that both models can support domestic SME financing through real-time payments, alternative data, and embedded credit. However, their capacity to enable cross-border SME finance depends on interoperability, data portability, legal recognition, and regulatory alignment. The article contributes to the literature by reframing digital payments as socio-technical information infrastructures rather than neutral settlement rails. It also offers a diagnostic framework for policymakers, central banks, FinTech firms, development institutions, and financial regulators seeking to design inclusive and interoperable SME finance ecosystems. The article concludes by proposing a research and policy agenda focused on open finance, cross-border data-recognition standards, SME usability, and infrastructure investment.

title: The Renewal Trap: How Perishable Data Stocks Delay Incumbent Adaptation
affiliations: HEC Paris - Strategy & Business Policy

detail.title: The Renewal Trap: How Perishable Data Stocks Delay Incumbent Adaptation
detail.abstract: When is satisfactory performance a misleading signal of organizational capability? I theorize a renewal trap: a form of resource-induced adaptation delay that arises when current performance is sustained by a depreciating inherited resource whose future value depends on renewal capability. I develop the argument in the context of data-driven competition. In datadriven markets, accumulated data can improve prediction and personalization, but its usefulness decays as users, products, technologies, and competitive conditions change. This creates a performance-feedback problem. Current performance can reflect stock health, the remaining value of old data, rather than renewal health, the ability to turn current interactions into useful new data. As a result, satisfactory performance may suppress attention to renewal precisely when future advantage requires it. A simple formal model isolates this mechanism. Inherited stock advantage persists only when renewal flows offset depreciation. When rivals have stronger renewal capability, they can overcome inherited stock disadvantages. Most importantly, incumbent vulnerability is highest not when data depreciate fastest, but when data depreciate slowly enough to sustain current performance yet quickly enough to erode future advantage. I illustrate the argument with public display-advertising data, showing that older campaign data predict current outcomes less well. This pattern gives empirical content to data depreciation, a key boundary condition of the theory. The paper reframes performance feedback as a diagnostic problem: when inherited resources depreciate slowly, success can conceal the erosion of renewal capability.

title: IPSAS Adoption and Financial Management in Public Universities in Nigeria

detail.title: IPSAS Adoption and Financial Management in Public Universities in Nigeria
detail.abstract: The broad objective of the study is to examine the impact of IPSAS adoption on financial management in public Universities using the University of Benin as case study. The data was generated using well-structured questionnaire while the structural equation model (SEM) was used as method of data analysis. A total sample of 40 respondents was used. The questionnaire covered sub areas of transparency, accountability, faithful representation and relevance which are all dimensions of financial management. Looking at the path analysis, the effect from IPSAS adoption in terms of accountability was found to be positive (0.38) and significant at 5%, the effect of IPSAS adoption on financial transparency (TRANP) in financial reporting in Nigerian universities was positive (0.38) and significant at 5%. Furthermore, the effect of IPSAS on the relevance of financial reporting in Nigerian universities (REL) was positive (0.46) and significant at 5%. Furthermore, the effect of IPSAS on faithful representation (FREP) in financial reporting in Nigerian universities reporting was positive (0.42) and significant at 5%. On the overall, the results suggest that IPSAS adoption has a positive impact on financial reporting quality in public universities. The study recommends the need for universities to fully comply with IPSAS requirements in its entire ramification so as to further improve the overall quality of financial reporting.

detail.abstract: This paper asks a practical question: can a machine-learning (ML) screen, built only from the data and tools an ordinary Indian retail investor can actually get hold of, pick stocks better than the priceto-earnings and price-to-book rules that retail investors have leaned on for decades? To answer it, I assemble a stratified sample of 50 companies drawn from five sectors of the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and train a Random Forest classifier on six fundamental and momentum features. The model is benchmarked against a conventional P/E and P/B screen over a 2023 hold-out year, with the model trained on the 2020-2022 cross-sections. On the test set the Random Forest reached a precision of 0.58 in identifying top-quartile return stocks, against 0.44 for the traditional screen and 0.25 for random selection. The advantage was not uniform. It was largest in less-researched mid-cap segments such as information technology and pharmaceuticals, and almost disappeared among large, heavily covered banking stocks where prices already reflect public fundamentals. A hypothetical equal-weighted portfolio of the model's picks returned 28.4 percent gross over 2023, versus 21.6 percent for the screen and 18.9 percent for the Nifty 500. The gap narrows once realistic transaction costs and the single-year test window are taken into account. I am candid about the things that limit these numbers-survivorship bias, an imperfect look-ahead lag, patchy mid-cap fundamentals, and a sample far too small to settle the question-and I argue that the honest takeaway is modest but real: with careful feature engineering, freely available ML can give the Indian retail investor a measurable edge, most of which can be captured by a simple multi-factor checklist that adds quality and momentum to the old value ratios.

detail.abstract: Implied volatility is obtained by numerically inverting an option pricing model and is typically reported as a scalar value without information about the reliability of the underlying computation. In the presence of bid–ask spreads, the standard Vega-based approximation of implied volatility uncertainty assumes a local linearity that can break down when curvature is material. This paper introduces a perturbation-conditioned diagnostic, 𝐸SGNIE, derived from the second-order expansion of the inverse pricing function, which quantifies the relative nonlinear error in Vega-based implied volatility uncertainty estimates. We further define a complementary absolute correction, 𝜖VP, expressed in volatility points, and show that implied volatility uncertainty admits a two-component decomposition into magnitude and nonlinear distortion. Empirical validation across five market regimes—spanning calm conditions, moderate stress, idiosyncratic volatility events, and systemic crises—and 27 underlying assets, covering 14,562 contracts, demonstrates that the SGNIE metric accurately captures nonlinear error. Across regimes and assets, SGNIE exhibits near-perfect rank correlation with realized nonlinear error magnitudes, high explanatory power, and stable calibration within well-conditioned regions of the pricing surface. Regression slopes below unity indicate that SGNIE tends to produce systematically larger nonlinear-error estimates than those realized, consistent with its interpretation as a conservative diagnostic derived from a truncated Taylor expansion. The joint distribution of 𝐸SGNIE and 𝜖VP shows that large nonlinear distortions are typically associated with large absolute corrections, while cases of high relative error with negligible magnitude are extremely rare: in the full validated sample, only 2 of 14,562 contracts satisfy 𝐸SGNIE ≥ 0.25 and 𝜖VP < 0.5. The SGNIE framework is diagnostic rather than predictive. It characterizes the reliability of implied volatility estimates under observed perturbations and integrates into existing pricing pipelines as a reliability annotation without altering the underlying inversion. The results provide a structured approach to identifying when linear approximations are valid and when they materially understate uncertainty.

title: Interest Rates and Private Investment in Haiti: A Cointegration Analysis
affiliations: Centre de Techniques de Planification et d’Économie Appliquée (CTPEA) and Centre de Techniques de Planification et d’Économie Appliquée (CTPEA), Centre de Techniques de Planification et d’Économie Appliquée (CTPEA)

detail.title: Interest Rates and Private Investment in Haiti: A Cointegration Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper provides a cointegration-based assessment of the relationship between the nominal interest rate and private investment in Haiti, using annual data over 1992-2015-the period during which the rate has been determined on the money market, after the abrogation of the regulated floor in February 1992. Augmented Dickey-Fuller and Phillips-Perron tests establish that both series are integrated of order one, and the Johansen procedure identifies a single cointegrating relationship under the appropriate deterministic specification. The estimated long-run elasticity implies that a one-percentage-point increase in the nominal interest rate is associated with a 0.35% decline in real private investment. A vector error correction model confirms a significant and negative short-run effect; Granger and Toda-Yamamoto tests document bidirectional causality; and a variance decomposition indicates that, on average over an 18-year horizon, around 48% of the variability of private investment is attributable to interest-rate innovations. The results are robust to the use of the real rather than the nominal rate, to the exclusion of the 1992-1995 embargo years, to the augmentation of the model by GDP, to a single-equation conditional ECM, and to a Gregory-Hansen test for cointegration with an endogenous structural break. These findings support the classical inverse-relationship hypothesis in a Caribbean low-income setting and have direct implications for the conduct of monetary policy by the Bank of the Republic of Haiti.

title: Institutional Drift: Why Coherence Erodes Before High-Stakes Organizations Fail
affiliations: Hoopoe Holding Ltd.

detail.title: Institutional Drift: Why Coherence Erodes Before High-Stakes Organizations Fail
detail.abstract: High-stakes organizations rarely fail in a single moment. More often, they drift. Before collapse becomes visible, coherence has already begun to erode through small losses in meaning, authority, memory, and responsibility. This paper argues that institutional failure is typically preceded by institutional drift, a gradual weakening of the internal structures that allow organizations to remain intelligible to themselves. In healthcare clinics, franchise systems, and other regulated service organizations, drift becomes visible when roles overlap without clarity, when decisions lose their proper home, when feedback fails to return to an accountable owner, and when organizational language no longer corresponds to operational reality. Existing explanations often treat failure as a problem of leadership, culture, or execution. While each matters, these accounts do not fully explain why well-resourced organizations can continue functioning while steadily losing coherence. This paper offers a diagnostic argument that reframes failure as the outcome of accumulated misalignment rather than abrupt breakdown. Drawing on earlier work on structural blindness, structural DNA, invisible governance, and relational alienation, the paper conceptualizes drift as the slow separation of organization from meaning (Barzegar, 2025a, 2025b, 2025c, 2025d). The contribution is theoretical. It identifies coherence erosion as the pre-failure condition that organizations often normalize until collapse becomes difficult to reverse.

detail.abstract: A sell-side process is usually decided on the highest letter of intent, on the assumption that the headline number is the number the seller will receive. It is rarely the number the seller receives. A signed letter of intent is non-binding, a material share of signed letters never reach close, and conditional on closing the price is routinely revised downward through purchase-price adjustments, escrows, and earnouts that now appear in the large majority of private-target deals. This paper defines the gap between a headline offer and its expected realized value as the Deal Certainty Discount and develops it as an organizing framework rather than a measured result. The empirical inputs are drawn from the cross-market M&A deal-terms and bidding-strategy literature, so the lower-middle-market claims are advanced as testable propositions rather than segment-specific measurements. Its central proposition is that offer aggressiveness raises both the risk of failure and the expected post-signing compression while process competition lowers both, so that the highest headline bid is frequently the least certain, and ranking offers by headline rather than by expected realized value can invert a seller's choice. The discount is the execution-stage component of the founder-to-close gap documented in prior Cordis Institute work, and the paper proposes a two-stage framework for where lower-middle-market value leaks.

detail.abstract: We investigate the competitive consequences of government financial assistance by examining non-assisted firms operating in the same product market as assisted firms. Using a novel dataset of U.S. federal, state, and local government assistance to U.S. public firms, we find that increases in government assistance to competitors are associated with a 12.2% decrease in nonassisted firms' financial performance. The decline in financial performance is driven by decreasing revenues and increasing research and development expenses. Results are more pronounced for financially constrained firms, and concentrated in permanent government assistance in the form of cash grants, cost reimbursements, and tax abatements/credits (rather than temporary assistance in the form of loans). We further show that greater competitor assistance is associated with a 5.1% decline in market share, particularly in less competitive markets. Overall, the evidence indicates that government assistance generates negative competitive externalities for non-assisted firmsa potentially unintended and previously unexplored consequence of government intervention that benefits some firms at the competitive expense of others.

detail.abstract: Amid intensifying U.S.–China strategic competition, the global spread of de-risking, protectionist industrial policies, and economic security regulations is accelerating a structural reconfiguration of global value chains and supply networks. In strategic sectors linked to critical minerals, energy, advanced components and equipment, and digital and green transitions, major economies are increasingly prioritizing supply chain resilience and economic security alongside cost efficiency. detail.abstract: The U.S. credit union system is large in aggregate but highly uneven by institution size. As of Dec. 31, 2025, credit unions with less than $100 million in assets accounted for 58.6 percent of federally insured credit unions but only 3.1 percent of system assets. [5] For this segment, liquidity readiness is less about systemic asset concentration and more about ensuring that smaller institutions can maintain member services, execute contingency funding plans (CFP), and produce supervisory reviewable evidence during stress. NCUA Regulation § 741.12 establishes tiered liquidity planning requirements based on asset size, including written liquidity policies, contingency funding plans (CFP), and for larger credit unions, documented access to at least one contingent federal liquidity source. [1] Building from these requirements and related NCUA liquidity risk guidance, this paper develops a practitioner framework for assessing liquidity readiness in smaller U.S. credit unions. The framework organizes liquidity readiness into six dimensions: governance and policy structure, liquidity measurement, stress scenario design, contingency funding capacity, board and ALCO reporting, and remediation evidence. The paper's contribution is methodological and practical. It converts dispersed regulatory and supervisory expectations into a source mapped assessment structure that can be used for self-assessment, advisor review, board and ALCO discussion, and examination preparation. An open-source toolkit implements the framework through a source map, readiness scorecard, policy-to-procedure traceability table, funding capacity worksheet, stress scenario calculator, board reporting template, and examiner preparation checklist. The toolkit is available at Credit Union Liquidity Readiness Toolkit, with source code and documentation at Credit Union Liquidity Management, and requires no proprietary credit union data.

detail.abstract: In the first weeks of 2026, roughly two trillion dollars in market capitalization disappeared from the U.S. software sector. The consensus explanation is that artificial intelligence disrupted the subscription model. This paper asks the prior question: were these valuations ever justified? Drawing on a panel of 115 publicly traded U.S. software companies tracked from 2016 through 2025, we argue that the SaaS sector constructed a financial architecture that allowed it to present results systematically disconnected from the underlying economics of its businesses. The central mechanism is the exclusion of stock-based compensation, the sector's largest routinely excluded cost, from the adjusted figures the market used to value these firms. Over the decade the sector expensed $153 billion in stock-based compensation while excluding it from reported performance, carried more than $320 billion in cumulative paid-in capital on its balance sheets by 2025, and accumulated roughly $75 billion in net losses. Across the panel the median GAAP operating margin was negative while the median adjusted margin, with that cost removed, was positive. We trace this permission structure to a four-decade genealogy in which useful financial conventions migrated beyond their original purpose, and we show how zero interest rate policy suppressed the market's incentive to question it. The beneficiaries sat inside the system that measured performance; the costs fell on the passive holders outside it. AI did not destroy two trillion dollars of value. It revealed that much of it was never there.

title: It's the Currency, Not the Rate: How the Fed Really Hurts Emerging Markets

detail.title: It's the Currency, Not the Rate: How the Fed Really Hurts Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: When the US Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy, the conventional fear is that rising US interest rates directly increase borrowing costs for emerging market governments. Using quarterly data from 23 emerging market economies over 2002-2024, this article shows that the direct effect of Federal Funds Rate changes on sovereign spreads is statistically insignificant. The operative transmission channel is the exchange rate: a 10 percent currency depreciation is associated with approximately 21.6 basis points of sovereign spread widening. Country-level analysis reveals sharp heterogeneity-Pakistan and Sri Lanka show the strongest positive responses while Malaysia, Thailand, and Poland show near-zero sensitivity. The policy implication is clear: exchange rate management and dollar liability reduction, not domestic interest rate policy, are the primary buffers against Fed tightening spillovers.

detail.abstract: This paper reports a 70-day pre-registered field experiment of Judgement Architecture (JA), a formal operating discipline for making human Judgement explicit, assigned, and enforceable at the points in AI-enabled workflows where decisions become consequential. Two JA-governed agents were deployed on Moltbook, a public platform where AI agents interact autonomously, between 16 March and 24 May 2026. Seven measurement dimensions were specified before deployment (pre-registration at SSRN 6428218): identity stability, boundary architecture, memory and trust governance, provenance and traceability, reasoning legibility, value propagation, and avoided commitment record. Findings: five dimensions met their pre-registered confirmation criteria; reasoning legibility was disconfirmed against the binary criterion; value propagation returned an inconclusive result with an exploratory visibility sub-finding. The experiment also captured two distinct failure arcs under live adversarial conditions: a five-day sequence of reasoning-mediated rule failure that produced a three-layer constraint architecture, and a late-experiment credential exposure through a helper agent whose instructions lacked the relevant rule. To the author's knowledge, this is the first pre-registered longitudinal field study of an architecture for engineering accountability into autonomous AI agents under live adversarial conditions. The architecture's holds and its failures are both documented, with the architectural responses to each failure organized for replication.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has two primary interactions with public procurement. First, procurement is the gateway for the still largely unregulated process of public sector AI adoption. Second, AI is being deployed to ‘streamline’ procurement itself. This contribution explores the competition implications of these interactions between AI and procurement, as well as the knock-on effects that AI-supported procurement can have on upstream markets. In particular, it considers competition implications of new procurement approaches concerning: the setting of technical and governance requirements; reliance on third party capabilities; unregulated AI audit and assurance mechanisms; unregulated practices such as the free embedding of AI solutions into contracted cloud or software solutions (or ‘AI creep’); as well as the risks of new forms of data bias, organisational conflicts of interest and centralisation forces arising from the deployment of AI solutions in procurement management (including ‘AI agents’). title: Fat Tails in Indian Equity Derivatives Market: Statistical Evidence and Systematic Exploitability in Bank Nifty

detail.title: Fat Tails in Indian Equity Derivatives Market: Statistical Evidence and Systematic Exploitability in Bank Nifty
detail.abstract: This study investigates the presence and exploitability of fat-tail phenomena in Indian equity derivatives market using Bank Nifty as the primary instrument for the analysis. Bank Nifty was selected because of its high volatility, concentrated sectoral composition and its important role in India's derivatives ecosystem. The study consists of statistical analysis of 1733 daily Bank Nifty returns and empirical study of intraday trading performance on 5 min and 30 min timeframes for the period February 2018 to February 2025. Daily returns show a negative skewness of-1.25 and an excess kurtosis of 124.08 and a Jarque-Bera statistic in excess of 1,110,000, all providing strong evidence against Gaussian behaviour. Events over three standard deviations were found 26 times, or about 5.56 times more than expected of a normal distribution. Even after excluding the most extreme 1% of observations, the excess kurtosis was still 31.06, confirming that fat-tail behaviour is a structural feature of the market, rather than being due to isolated market crises. A fully mechanical, pivot-based trading system was tested on over 4,500 intraday observations. The 30 minute implementation generated 19,434 net points with annualised returns of 17.23%(per annum) and a Sharpe Ratio of 0.965. The 5 minute implementation generated 16915 net points with annualised returns of 8.12%. The profitability was heavily concentrated in a small number of extreme winning trades, confirming that fat-tail events can be systematically exploited. With a conservative cost assumption of 24 points per completed trade, transaction costs reduced theoretical profitability by 49.28% in the 30 minute strategy and 84.27% in the 5 minute strategy. The study adds to the limited literature on fat-tail behaviour in Indian financial markets, and broadens evidence that extreme events can be modelled with structured trading frameworks with major implications for risk management, derivatives pricing and market regulation.

detail.abstract:
This paper defines a structural tendency operating across human systems: accountability erodes whenever work moves, scales, or continues without active maintenance. The tendency has been described in pieces for decades, by Drucker, Deming, Christensen, Simon, Arendt, Thompson, Perrow, Reason, Vaughan, Meadows, Beck, and Herzog and colleagues, each from within a single field. Each field studies it as a separate problem under its own name; the accounts have not been brought together as one phenomenon. This paper defines it as Responsibility Erosion and isolates the specific form made acute by AI and automation: Judgement Decay, in which work crosses a structural boundary and accountability does not cross with it.
Evidence is presented across three lines: convergent observations across the better part of a century of scholarship, the historical record of how accountability has been maintained (and lost) at each scale of human organization, and a pre-registered field study of one architectural response to Judgement Decay (Husk, 2026c). Recognition scenarios from current AI-enabled work open the argument; they are illustrations, not evidence. Five objections are addressed: that accountability self-corrects, that the phenomenon is already named elsewhere, that this is AI risk under a broader label, that the empirical base is thin, and that the paper prescribes while claiming to describe. The contribution is defining and isolating: one definition connects what many fields have each described in part, and the isolated form gives researchers and designers a specific point to work on.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic method for global value chain (GVC) analysis, moving beyond static frameworks that decompose nominal variables, such as gross exports or value added. Instead, it breaks down year-by-year real economic growth, considering contributions from value-added sources, final producers, users, and different types of value chains: pure domestic, traditional trade, and simple and complex GVCs. The approach, based on inputoutput theory, is demonstrated with a numerical example, applied to the WIOD and Long-run WIOD datasets to create the GVC Growth Contribution Database (GVC-GCD). Preliminary analyses with the GVC-GCD offer new insights into GVC growth, revealing that GVCs predate the term and influence global growth steadily over time despite short-term fluctuations, differences between large and small, developed and developing, more specialised or diversified economies. With few exceptions, growth contributions, including those of international ones, have decreased over time. In the long run, while trade and GVCs benefited many countries, they could not fully offset the decline in the contributions of domestic value chains. This historical perspective offers lessons for current policy. The GVC-GCD can serve as a tool for future empirical studies and growth modelling, with potential to expand across space, time, and levels of detail as data availability improves.

detail.abstract: Design buildability is an important aspect of Design for Manufacture and Assembly (DfMA) to examine the sequence of building or construction activities, prefabrication opportunities, and onsite assembly. The lack of tight integration between the assembly process and existing digital solutions, however, is a significant gap in onsite sequencing and assembly. This paper explores the critical factors for Building Information Modelling (BIM) based principles and other digital technologies that can support DfMA for appropriate decision-making in onsite sequencing and assembly. The literature review reveals the existing approaches to onsite sequencing and assembly (OSA), as well as identifies their missing key capabilities/features. Although BIM-based initiatives exist for various construction purposes, BIM for onsite sequencing and assembly has not received the required attention from academia and industry, and a qualitative study was conducted to understand gaps in construction sequencing, onsite assembly practices, and industry practitioners' expectations. The study identified 14 factors for streamlining onsite sequencing and assembly using existing BIM capabilities or principles, categorising them into four groups based on their relationships and interconnections. The study's findings are expected to enhance understanding of BIM principles and other technologies for onsite sequencing and assembly among construction professionals, including contributing to the existing knowledge of onsite assembly in a BIM environment.

detail.abstract: The UK AI Compass is a large-scale segmentation of British public opinion on artificial intelligence. Drawing on a nationally representative survey of 2,911 UK adults (2,774 weighted), with oversamples of ethnic-minority and marginal-constituency voters, and five focus groups held across the nations and regions, it finds a public that has already formed strong, largely protective views on AI. Eighty-five per cent want stronger laws to make AI safe, and majorities favour regulation across most policy trade-offs. detail.title: The Business Owner as a Semi-Stillness Investor
detail.abstract: Prior work in this research program established semi-stillness as a yield-enhanced strategy that functions as a short put: long asset plus yield (Aktaş, 2026c). This paper applies that framework to private business ownership. A business owner holds a long position in their company (the asset) and collects net income (the yield). Unlike public stocks, where price and earnings can diverge due to sentiment, private business valuation is typically a multiple of earnings, creating a tight link between income and asset price. This paper makes four contributions. First, it provides a mathematical proof that income decrease creates net real loss even when nominal income remains positive, with the threshold determined by the valuation multiple. Second, it shows that semi-stillness for business requires directional positioning for income growth-a long call on income growth. Third, it maps business strategy to the two primitives: Mean Reversion (fix undervalued businesses) and Momentum (ride high-growth sectors). Fourth, it analyzes private equity and venture capital as portfolio-level applications of these strategies. The paper concludes with implications for the planned Political Systematical Business book.

detail.abstract:
Geopolitical tensions and open conflict in West Asia encompassing Israel, Iran, the Gulf monarchies, and adjacent maritime chokepoints such as the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Suez Canal have re-emerged as a central risk to the global economy between 2023 and 2026. These conflicts have coincided with, and interacted with, existing stresses from the Russia-Ukraine war, post-pandemic inflation, and climate-related disruptions to create a layered shock to energy markets, maritime logistics, and financial conditions. This paper investigates how current and prospective escalations in West Asia affect global growth, inflation, trade, and corporate performance through the intertwined channels of energy prices, supply-chain fragmentation, capital flows, and risk sentiment. Methodologically, it combines a selective review of recent literature on geopolitical risk and macroeconomic dynamics with an event-study perspective on earlier conflicts including the 1973 oil embargo, the Gulf and Iraq wars, the Arab Spring, and the Russia-Ukraine war and draws on up-to-date data from the IMF, IEA, UNCTAD, and other institutions through May 2026. 

The key findings are fivefold. First, energy-price shocks arising from West Asia conflicts remain the dominant first-round transmission channel, but their macro impact now strongly depends on the credibility of monetary policy and the responsiveness of shale and non-OPEC supply. Second, maritime disruptions in the Red Sea–Suez and Hormuz corridors have transformed from short-lived logistical events into persistent supply-chain reconfigurations, raising shipping costs, lengthening delivery times, and reallocating trade routes. Third, sectoral effects are highly heterogeneous: defence contractors, cybersecurity firms, and some hydrocarbon exporters benefit from higher demand and risk premia, while energy-intensive manufacturers, airlines, and maritime-dependent retailers face compressed margins and volatile cash flows. Fourth, emerging markets exposed through energy imports, remittances, and tourism including India experience a complex mix of terms-of-trade deterioration, imported inflation, and selective opportunities from supply-chain diversification. Finally, corporate resilience hinges on active geopolitical risk management, diversified sourcing, digital visibility across supply chains, and credible ESG and governance architectures that can withstand investor scrutiny in an era of fragmentation.

Policy implications follow on three levels. For governments and central banks, the imperative is to balance targeted energy and social support with medium-term fiscal sustainability, while guarding inflation expectations and monitoring financial-stability spillovers from sudden stops in capital flows. For corporations, the evidence supports strategic redundancy in critical inputs, multi-regional production footprints, and dynamic capital allocation across scenarios rather than static cost-minimisation. For institutional investors and regulators, the West Asia conflict underscores the need to embed geopolitical risk, supply-chain resilience, and transition-aligned energy strategies within ESG taxonomies, stewardship codes, and disclosure standards. The paper concludes that West Asia conflict risk is likely to be a semi-permanent feature of the global landscape, requiring an anticipatory, rather than reactive, approach to macroeconomic stabilisation and corporate strategy.

title: Slide or Feed: Recommendation Layout, Monetization, and Data-Driven Learning

detail.title: Slide or Feed: Recommendation Layout, Monetization, and Data-Driven Learning
detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly use recommender systems not only to select content but also to determine who completes the matching process: the algorithm or the viewer. We study recommendation layout as a strategic design choice that allocates residual matching authority between the platform's algorithm and viewers. In a slide interface, viewers consume one algorithmically selected item at a time, largely delegating matching to the platform. In a feed interface, viewers observe multiple recommended items and screen among them, retaining part of the matching task. We develop a model of a content platform that chooses its recommendation layout and advertising load while the recommendation quality improves with viewer-generated data. The model identifies a tradeoff between algorithmic delegation and viewer-side screening. Feed improves realized match quality when recommendations are imprecise or content supply is sparse, while slide reduces browsing and decision frictions when the platform's matching environment is strong. A key implication is that the engagement-maximizing layout need not be revenue-maximizing: in intermediate matching environments, slide may generate more consumption, while feed generates higher advertising revenue by increasing the value of consumed attention and viewers' tolerance for ads. A dynamic extension shows that forward-looking platforms moderate early advertising and may transition from feed to slide as data and content supply improve. The results position recommendation layout as a strategic information-systems design choice that shapes matching, monetization, and platform learning.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: In this paper, we introduce and define the supply chain butterfly effect through the example of the US retailing industry. The supply chain butterfly effect captures the financial impact of supply chain and operations, which presents a long-standing question yet fully answered by the theory and practice of supply chains, operations and finance.

Methodology/results: Using the example of the US retailing industry from 2016 to 2025, we discover and quantify the supply chain butterfly effect, defined to be an economic phenomenon where a change in supply chains can lead to a proportionately larger change in companies’ financial performance and market value, analogous to the well-known butterfly effect where a butterfly flapping its wing may cause a massive storm. The supply chain butterfly effect works through a two-step chain reaction: A change in supply chains can be amplified on the financials, e.g., net income, through the supply chain multiplier. The change of net income can be further amplified in the stock market into a proportionally larger change in the market capitalization through the financial multiplier. Using revenue breakdown, simple linear regressions and panel data study, we estimate the median supply chain multiplier for the US retailing to be around 20, and the average financial multiplier to be 25, and thus the combined effect, to be 500.

Managerial implications: This paper illustrates the pathway through which supply chain operations can contribute to a retailing firm’s financial performance and market value. We show that a change in supply chains can be amplified by 500 times in the stock market for the US retailing. The supply chain butterfly effect allows us to prove the value of supply chain related jobs, establish the impact of the academic field of supply chain and operations management, and showcase to students why they should take related majors.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This paper develops a conceptual framework of the enablers driving the adoption of blockchain technology (BT) for traceability in the marine supply chain (MSC), with particular reference to the seafood export sector of a developing economy such as India. The framework proposes that a cluster of technological competence and readiness enablers, familiarity with blockchain operators, AI and data capabilities, the Internet of Things, willingness for training, and legal awareness can act as primary drivers that shape more dependent, outcome-side enablers such as trust, communication, and standardisation. Abstract:
Executive and organizational coaching literature has long positioned questioning as a facilitative communication skill — a conversational tool for stimulating reflection and behavioral change. This instrumental framing, however, leaves inquiry theoretically underdeveloped and obscures its constitutive role in reshaping leadership cognition and organizational sensemaking.
This article presents the Cognitive–Action Inquiry Matrix (CAIM), a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes structured inquiry as an epistemic intervention: a mechanism through which coaches systematically disrupt maladaptive cognitive schemas, surface governing assumptions, and enable systemic reframing. Drawing on dual-process cognition, double-loop learning, reflective practice, and predictive processing, CAIM organizes four inquiry architectures — LEGAL, LBAC, L-COACH, and LCMM — across two dimensions: cognitive depth and action orientation.
The framework advances five falsifiable theoretical propositions and operationalizes cognitive entropy — the persistence of conflicting or unresolved interpretive schemas in leadership cognition — as the central mechanism linking inquiry design to organizational learning outcomes. Boundary conditions governing framework applicability and a structured empirical research agenda are specified to guide future validation.

This paper asks a less comfortable question. When retailers, regulators and consumers all observe the same transparent price field, does transparency simply empower consumers, or does it also reshape the conditions for strategic pricing and market surveillance?

Using Sydney’s retail petrol market as a law-and-economics case study, this paper examines the interaction between price transparency, oligopolistic pricing behaviour and public market monitoring. The analysis combines Edgeworth price-cycle theory, Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) petroleum-market reports from 2023 to 2026, revised brand- and station-level price evidence, and a reproducible exercise using public NSW FuelCheck station-level data from Data.NSW. FuelCheck is treated not only as a consumer information tool for locating lower prices, searching by brand or fuel type, navigating to service stations and reporting price discrepancies to NSW Fair Trading, but also as market infrastructure that makes pricing behaviour more visible.

The paper documents repeated asymmetric pricing patterns in Sydney: sharp restorations, gradual discounting phases, station-level heterogeneity and incomplete synchronisation across brands. These dynamics are formalised using measures of retail-wholesale margins, cycle amplitude, relenting and discounting speed, lead-lag delay, anomaly screening and cost-side pass-through. ACCC evidence places the cycles within shifting wholesale-cost regimes shaped by terminal gate prices, Singapore Mogas 95, exchange-rate exposure, fuel excise changes and geopolitical shocks. A March 2026 FuelCheck exercise further demonstrates how public station-level data can be transformed into a reproducible daily average U91 price series for Sydney.

The paper does not allege cartel conduct, explicit collusion or unlawful price fixing. Its contribution is instead to show how transparent price infrastructure performs three overlapping functions: it facilitates consumer search, supports competition-policy surveillance and generates lessons for market design. The argument also extends beyond petrol. In increasingly transparent financial and tokenised markets, better visibility may improve access while increasing the need for surveillance tools capable of detecting liquidity fragmentation, price divergence and strategic behaviour.

title: PERM Compliance Checklist and Toolkit with AI-Assisted Workflows and Prompts

detail.title: PERM Compliance Checklist and Toolkit with AI-Assisted Workflows and Prompts
detail.abstract: This Article presents a practice-oriented toolkit for managing the PERM (Program Electronic Review Management) labor certification process under 20 C.F.R. Part 656. Organized around a six-phase framework-prevailing wage determination, job requirements and qualifications analysis, recruitment planning and documentation, recruitment report and applicant handling, ETA Form 9089 preparation and filing, and audit/RFI response and record retention-the toolkit provides checklists, templates, sample language, and scenario-based guidance designed for use by immigration paralegals under attorney supervision. It also integrates optional AI-assisted workflow prompts for drafting, consistency review, and scheduling tasks, subject to appropriate professional oversight. The toolkit addresses current practice challenges including FLAG system auto-population, O*NET Job Zone changes, OFLC program integrity measures (VIBE), and themes from the March 2026 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.

title: Village Productivity Index (VPI) / Indeks Produktivitas Desa (IPD): A New Framework for Measuring Rural Economic Contribution Beyond Administrative Performance

detail.title: Village Productivity Index (VPI) / Indeks Produktivitas Desa (IPD): A New Framework for Measuring Rural Economic Contribution Beyond Administrative Performance
